chapters.summary: Chair describes Brooklyn Public Library's October 6 event on artistic freedom, praises artist Christopher Mays and his stained-glass works and tapestries featuring banned book characters, and notes his father Walter Dean Myers.
chapters.title: Chair Williams highlights Brooklyn Public Library Banned Books Week event

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Before we hear about the resolutions and our oversight topic, let me say a few words about a perfect meetup of the arts and the libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It happened on October 6th when the Brooklyn Library held a noteworthy event at the Central Library commemorating Banned Books Week.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In February 2024, this committee held a hearing entitled New York City Libraries Fight Against Banning Books.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In that hearing, the committee honored the remarkable work that our libraries were doing to support the freedom to read for people throughout the U.S., not just here in our city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Our public libraries are still doing that work in the midst of an even more dire and repressive circumstance nationally, and we commend them for it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Brooklyn Public Library's October 6th event was entitled On Artistic Freedom.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It was a panel discussion by notable and award-winning visual and performing artists, producers, and publishers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All the panelists were outstanding as they spoke about censorship of artists and writers and performers in our current national climate.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I want to give a special shout-out to visual artist and children's book author and illustrator Christopher Mays.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Among many other works, Chris wrote and illustrated Black Cat, and I have the book.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's my new thing, bringing books.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Illustrated Black Cat as one of the best children's books ever.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Now his newest works are displayed throughout the lobby of Brooklyn Central Library.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They are a series of large stained glass works that capture a group of New York City kids bicycling past the landmarks of the city with a

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: kind of youthful exuberance and freedom of collective movement under the night sky.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In the words of the library, these literally brilliant works are represented on paper in Chris's newest children's book entitled Night Ride.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Further, Chris has made 20 40 feet tapestries, which are also on display.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: On them, you can see giant characters from well-known banned books, reminding us what can be lost when books are banned in schools and public libraries across the country.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As Chris said, it was important to him that his art be displayed not just in museums, but also in a public library, because he was, as he said, born into book worlds.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: His father was the late and very great young adult books author Walter D.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Myers, with whom Chris worked on the well-known book-long poetic masterpiece Harlem, among other projects.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Our committee is especially happy this month that our purview is both culture and libraries because what a pair they make.

chapters.summary: Farah Louis explains her personal connection to reggaeton as a dancer, traces its Afro-Caribbean and Panamanian roots, and urges support for designating October as Reggaeton Heritage Month in NYC.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis presents Resolution 625 on Reggaeton Heritage Month

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Now let me invite Councilmember Lewis to speak about her resolution.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker and Chair Williams, for your leadership and for championing this resolution through the committee.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Today, I am proud and generally excited to bring forward Resolution 625, designating October as Reggaeton Heritage Month in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And I want to tell you why this one is personal to me and some advocates that we have here in the room today.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Gregorio Mayers, founder of the Panamanian 507 Roundtable, and Dr.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Mita from the Evanita Records.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I grew up in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I was a dancer, and as a dancer, I had to learn every genre of music to choreograph routines and showcases, from jazz to hip-hop to Latin styles.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And reggaeton was not optional.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It was essential.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Reggaeton builds body isolations, rhythmic musicality, and dynamic hip mobility that translates across every urban and Latin style there is.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: During undergrad at LIU Brooklyn, my classmates and I didn't just enjoy reggaeton, we studied it.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Our professors integrated it into our modern dance curriculum because it belongs there.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It is a rich, cultural, layered, and physically demanding art form that deserves to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And that tradition continues right now on college campuses across the city, LIU Brooklyn, NYU Tandon.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Pratt, Brooklyn College students are all gathering, networking, and building community around the guillotine.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It is not just music, it's a cultural home.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: But this resolution is also about honoring where it all began.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: In the 1980s, Afro-Caribbeans in Panama took Jamaican reggae and dancehall and translated it into Spanish, giving birth to reggae espanol.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Pioneers like El General, Chico Man, Carlito Sol, and Granato laid a foundation that would change music forever.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: When El General came to New York City, he worked with Caribbean producers to craft the fusion of dance hall, reggae, and hip-hop.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: That world would come to be known as reggaeton.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Puerto Rican icons Daddy Yankee, Ivy Queen, Bad Bunny carried that legacy to every corner of the globe.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: New York City was part of that story, and it is time we made that official.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Reggaeton is a symbol of cultural identity.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It is an economic powerhouse for Latin music.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It is a platform for social and political expression.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: It is a living history that all New Yorkers deserve to learn, celebrate, and carry forward.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: We owe it to our Panamanian, Puerto Rican, and Afro-Caribbean communities to enshrine that recognition right here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: to support Resolution 625.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams celebrates the Shangri-Las as a Queens girl group with six top 40 hits, then explains Kwanzaa's origins, seven principles, and her resolution to make it a public holiday in New York.
chapters.title: Chair Williams speaks on Shangri-Las and Kwanzaa resolutions

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Now, let me say a few words about my resolutions as well.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Was there a greater girl group of the 1960s than the Shangri-La?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Those of us from Queens and their fans around the world would argue that there was not.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Lead vocalist Mary Weiss and her older sister Betty, who was the sole surviving member of the group, teamed up with the twins Marge and Mary Ann at Andrew Jackson High School in Cambria Heights, which is in my district, and made history with their Billboard Hot 100

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: number one hit, Leader of the Pack, in November 1964.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They knocked the Supremes'Baby Love out of number one spot.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The Shangri-La had six top 40 singles between 1964 and 1966, starting in the summer of 1964 with Remember Walking in the Sand, which climbed to number five on the Billboard Hot 100 and gave audiences its memorable, wrenching...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm not reading this out loud.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no lyric.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The Shangri-La, four teenagers from Queens, I'm going to kill Regina, because she created this, have influenced vocalists for the past 60 years, from the Ramones to Debbie Harry to Amy Winehouse.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: No one did it better.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Kwanzaa is an African-American and Pan-African holiday honoring African history, culture, family, and community.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The word Kwanzaa comes from the Swahili words meaning first fruits and refers to the harvest festival celebrated in Africa.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Kwanzaa was created in 1966 by Dr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Karinga, chair of Africana Studies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: At California State University in Long Beach and founder of the African American Cultural Center.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In his annual Kwanzaa message in December 2024, Karinga wrote that during Kwanzaa, we practiced a ritual of candle lighting called lifting up the light that lasts,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: based not only on the history of our people and practice, but also from the sacred teachings of our ancestors.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Karinga explained the seven principles of Kwanzaa, which are unity, self-determination, collective work and responsibility, cooperative economics, purpose, creativity, and faith.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In 2012, President Obama wrote that Kwanzaa serves as a time of reflection, taking lessons learned from our past and looking forward to a more promised tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: He wrote that we must recommit ourselves to building a country where all Americans have the opportunity to achieve their dreams.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Making Kwanzaa the seven-day period beginning December 26 and ending January 1,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: a public holiday for all New Yorkers statewide would reaffirm our state's commitment to diversity while designating a time for celebrating and preserving African Americans'heritage and honoring their contributions to the cultural, political, and economic life of all New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether CreateNYC lived up to its promise of cultural equity, noting artists struggle with affordability, small organizations fight to stay open, and communities face barriers to funding and resources.
chapters.title: Chair Williams frames CreateNYC oversight questions

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Finally, let me turn to the topic of our oversight hearing, what's next for Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As everyone in this room knows, New York City is the cultural capital of the world, not by accident, but because generations of creative visionaries have made this city their home.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: From Broadway to the Bronx, from world-renowned museums to neighborhood theaters, community art,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: art centers, and grassroots cultural institutions, our city's creative spirit is woven into the fabric of who we are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In 2017, in an attempt to develop a comprehensive citywide cultural plan worthy of its peerless cultural community,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: New York City adopted Create New York City with a bold promise that the arts would not be a privilege reserved for a select few, but a public good accessible to every New Yorker in every borough and in every neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Nearly a decade later, that law that established Create NYC gives us an opportunity to reexamine the plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So the time has come for us to ask a fundamental question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Has Create NYC lived up to its promise?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because while New York City's cultural institutions continue to inspire the world, the people who make our city extraordinary are facing extraordinary challenges.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Artists are struggling to afford the neighborhoods they help shape.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Small cultural organizations are fighting to keep their doors open, and too many communities still face barriers to the funding, resources, and opportunities that allow arts and culture to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cultural equity cannot simply be a phrase in a planning document or a promise made at a press conference.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It must be reflected in where we invest, whose voices we elevate, whose stories we tell, and who gets to participate in the cultural life of our city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Today's hearing is an opportunity to examine what Create NYC has accomplished, where it has fallen short, and whether

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: whether the city has established the accountability and measurable outcomes necessary to revamp the city's cultural plan and turn it from a bold vision into lasting change.

chapters.summary: Mark Stern introduces himself and Susan Seifert, explains SIAP's founding in 1994, and argues cultural opportunities are part of community well-being, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Mark Stern introduces SIAP and its community well-being framework

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: My name is Mark Stern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: I'm a professor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Professor, is it on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Nope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: I'm still Mark Stern, and I'm a professor of social policy and history at the University of Pennsylvania.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: My name's Susan Seifert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: I'm a colleague of Mark, a city planner and social urban community research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: My colleague Susan Seifert and I founded Penn's Social Impact of the Arts Project in 1994 to analyze culture's contribution to community well-being in Philadelphia and other cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We're completing our second study of New York currently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We'd like to summarize some of our findings and their implications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Much of the discussion of culture in the United States now focuses on its economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: By contrast, SIAP, Social Impact of the Arts Project, our value proposition sees cultural opportunities as an important aspect of community well-being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: and as a contributor to other dimensions of well-being, including health, educational opportunities, and social connection, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In lower and moderate income neighborhoods, cultural engagement is a form of civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In many of these neighborhoods, what SIAP calls civic clusters, intentional social action by residents and local organizations allows otherwise disadvantaged communities to enjoy more cultural

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: engagement than their economic standing would lead us to expect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Over the past four years, we've accumulated a lot of data on more than 5,000 nonprofit cultural providers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: 15,000 for-profit cultural businesses, over a million cultural participant households, and data on 11 other dimensions of community well-being to look at the connection with the arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: To document existing cultural assets and measures community well-being for every New York neighborhood and examine how they influence each other.

chapters.summary: Stern describes a 'new geography of exclusion,' shows a steep relationship between economic well-being and cultural assets, and defines market, market-adjacent, and civic clusters like Brownsville and Flushing.
chapters.title: Mark Stern presents findings on cultural inequality and civic clusters

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The social impact of culture is embedded, however, in existing social structures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The explosion of economic inequality over the past generation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: has coalesced into what we call a new geography of exclusion that has tilted the playing field toward higher income residents in neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The graph on page one of the handout that we circulated gives a concise look at the structure of cultural inequality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The line shows the overall relationship between economic well-being and cultural assets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: As you can see, the line has a steep rise as you move from poorer to well-off neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The dots on that diagram represent particular neighborhoods that are members of one of the three

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: cultural clusters that we identified in our study.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Market and market clusters are affluent neighborhoods with at least an average number of cultural assets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Civic clusters represent lower and moderate income neighborhoods like Brownsville or Flushing with more cultural assets than their economic status would predict.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Civic clusters represent what we'd like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: every lower income neighborhood to have a vibrant cultural life, adequate cultural assets, and better health education and community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Most researchers and funders tend to focus on cultural organizations in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: SIAP uses the idea of a neighborhood cultural ecology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: to shift our attention from individual cultural providers to the density of cultural assets in the neighborhood because that density multiplies collective impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We found a lot of geographic change in cities' cultural ecology over the past decade, but little change in its overall economic structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In fact, overall, cultural assets are less equally distributed today than they were a decade ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Between 2016 and 2025, although Manhattan remained the dominant location of cultural assets in the city, many neighborhoods closed the gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The shift of resident artists from Manhattan to Brooklyn and Queens over the past decade was the most dramatic of these changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: As a number of artists living in Brooklyn and Queens, including neighborhoods like Spatz, Bed-Stuy, and Ridgewood,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: the number living in many Manhattan neighborhoods, and what you might think of as iconic arts neighborhoods, like Chelsea, the Upper West Side, and West Village declined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Yet, although its geography changed, the unequal distribution of cultural assets across New York's neighborhoods remained largely unchanged.

chapters.summary: Stern says DCLA funding shifts were swamped by inequality, describes four community well-being clusters, and finds cultural assets in lower-income neighborhoods correlate with fewer strokes, fewer low-weight births, and higher test scores.
chapters.title: Mark Stern links cultural assets to health and education outcomes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Although DCLA followed the cultural plan's recommendation to address the inequitable distribution of program funds to lower-income neighborhoods,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: These policy changes were swamped by the city's increased economic inequality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: As I mentioned, we used a variety of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: sources to calculate 11 dimensions of well-being in addition to cultural assets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: They range from economic well-being to health, school effectiveness, to environmental factors like pollution and heat vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We then use cluster analysis to identify four types of community well-being clusters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Central advantage, neighborhood advantage, diverse and struggling, and concentrated disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Many community well-being, although

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Sorry, many community well-being dimensions mirror neighborhoods'economic standing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In other words, residents'chances to enjoy good health, effective schools, and strong social connection are all associated with their neighborhoods'per capita income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Although most cultural clusters remained stable over the last decade, two sets shifted in notable ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: A number of neighborhoods in Brooklyn and Queens that had been disadvantaged or diverse and struggling became advantaged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And secondly, in addition, many neighborhoods, particularly some in central Brooklyn and eastern Queens, that had been concentrated disadvantage became diverse and struggling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The net effect was to reduce the number of concentrated

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: disadvantaged neighborhoods from 65 in 2016 to 52 in 2025,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: which resulted in the number of residents living in concentrated disadvantaged neighborhoods to fall from 3.1 million to 2.5 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In other words, over a half million fewer New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: live in a concentrated disadvantaged neighborhood than did so a decade ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: If we turn to the relationship of cultural assets to well-being, controls for social advantage, we found that among affluent neighborhoods, culture had no unique influence on measures of well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: But among lower income neighborhoods,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: we find significant and strong relationships between cultural assets and morbidity, birth outcomes, school effectiveness, and personal social connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: If we translate these statistics to examine individual risks and benefits, we find that compared to other

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: lower income neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Living in a low income neighborhood with more cultural assets leads to fewer strokes, fewer low weight births, and higher math and English and language arts scores.

chapters.summary: Stern reviews DCLA's CIG and CDF changes, recommends building from strength in civic clusters, and cites Bronx Council on the Arts, Queens Museum, and Kensington Cultural Council as examples of community capacity building.
chapters.title: Mark Stern urges DCLA to adopt a neighborhood-focused approach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Looking ahead, DCLA for most of its history has served as a means of funding individual nonprofit cultural providers through the Cultural Institutions Group and the Cultural Development Fund programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The 2018-2017 Cultural Plan called on the agency to use what we think of as a neighborhood lens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In allocating funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: As a result, the city expanded the CIGs to add members located outside of Manhattan

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: and shifted CDF funding to target neighborhoods identified by the city's Task Force on Racial Inclusion and Equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: An earmarked fund for underserved communities increased funding to about half of CDF grantees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Applying a neighborhood lens to funding program was a good first step, but the next phase may require the agency to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: rethink itself more thoroughly as a neighborhood-focused agency, including changes in how it operates internally, its relationship to other city and borough agencies, and the support for grassroots effort across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In terms of neighborhood focus, we learned a lot from one of our colleagues in Philadelphia, the Reinvestment Fund, a community development financial institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Their slogan is build from strength.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: That is to identify a neighborhood's strength and build links between it and other neighborhoods that are more vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We've learned that civic clusters are points of strength that the city could use to build other stronger neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In some ways, cultural providers and civic clusters are already doing this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We found that CDF grantees in civic cluster neighborhoods are connecting to other community-based organizations in their neighborhood more often than those in other neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We also found existing examples of cultural providers employing strategies to build community capacity, including community asset mapping, and here we noted

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: the Bronx Council on the Arts was working on this, employing community organizers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: To link community concerns to cultural expression.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Of course, Queens Museum began using that quite a while ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And finally, cultural organizing to activate neighborhood spaces with the Kensington Cultural Council in Brooklyn being an example of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We're likely to overlook the fact that cultural engagement is a public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: What are the economic consequences of fewer low-weight births or stronger social connection in a neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The economic consequences of these social impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: affect all New Yorkers, especially residents of lower and moderate income neighborhoods across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The city made a good choice in addressing the unequal distribution of cultural assets among neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: It can now build on that success by refining its approach to achieve a more just city

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: led by a more equitable cultural ecology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks what New York can learn from other cities, noting New York's size; Mark Stern contrasts vertical networks in New York with horizontal neighborhood networks in Philadelphia.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks SIAP about lessons from Philadelphia and other cities

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just have a few questions, and I appreciate your testimony and your research.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, you had testimony as well?

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: No, that was joint.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we understand you've worked in Philadelphia and other cities before your research in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Are there lessons you learned elsewhere that could be applied to New York?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I always put a caveat because New York is such a large city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, like Philly, it's like, I think Queens has more people than the whole city of Philly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I know it's like always a difficult conversation.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And, you know, but it's...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Sometimes as New Yorkers, we think we have all the answers, and we don't.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: People are doing some things better in other places.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wondering in your research if you think there's anything that could be applied to New York City or that New York City could learn from other cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Well, it is true that Philadelphia and New York are very different cities, and especially their cultural ecology are notable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In Philadelphia, one of our mayors, a couple of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: administrations ago just decided we didn't need an office on Odson culture and just close it down for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Fortunately, next month, the city's voting on a resolution to add the office to the city charter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: So that's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: One of the things when we were doing most of our original work was in Philadelphia and looking at the two cities together at one point it occurred to us that when we talk about social networks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: in New York it seemed like we were always talking about what we thought of as vertical networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: How did a local group connect up to his city council person?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: To the cultural affairs department, what have you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: In Philadelphia, we don't have that amount of resources, so groups don't spend that much time looking about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: What we found is that when they think about networks, they tend to be more horizontal networks, leading out to other groups in their neighborhood,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And that that's, and I guess what we realized is that would be something that we didn't see as much in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And that it would be great if they could complement those vertical networks with horizontal networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: Sue, did you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Just the horizontal networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: I mean, I think the ways Philadelphia and New York are different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: different is the lower and moderate income neighborhoods are more the experience we have throughout Philadelphia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: I mean, we have a full class society, blue bloods, whatever, but still the in the and I would say city council really represents a lot of connection with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: their districts and neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: So we were thinking that one lesson might be cultivate DCLA or cultivating or working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's not just with other cultural groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's neighborhood groups, community centers, rec centers, you know, business improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We saw this happening of necessity in Philadelphia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We're offering it to you like an idea, and it probably is happening, but we didn't pick it up in our research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: You know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Because that's really at the qualitative level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: That's also field work, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: And we're thinking, you know, you get out the door, you do some of this, you'll see it, you'll document it, and you'll...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Fund it, maybe more flexible types of funding than the CDF or, you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Because one of our things is flexible neighborhood funds, which means just small groups funding partnerships over just organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: So it's a combination of factors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: That may work in parts of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: not where New York is the world cultural capital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We're not doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's never where we were anyway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We're city people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We started in Philadelphia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's a dying city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We're so excited to have cities revive and people move back to all of these neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's a new

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: world and full of opportunity.

chapters.summary: Chair asks for more detail on civic clusters; Stern says they are lower-income neighborhoods with more cultural assets than expected, and Seifert explains the 'build from strength' model to support nearby vulnerable neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks SIAP to explain civic clusters and why Council should care

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So your testimony also calls attention to civic clusters.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you could just explain a little bit more about what that is and why should the city council take an interest in civic clusters?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: So, you know, in the diagram I pointed to earlier in my testimony, you can see civic clusters are, in a sense, lower income neighborhoods that have lots more cultural assets than we would predict.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: The reason we think they're important is because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: We think every lower income neighborhood ideally could become a civic cluster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And so we've sort of been held.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And so there's two parts of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: One is that it's easy because it's very easy to miss them because they are lower income neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mark Stern
utterances.text: And secondly, because we think if you change strategic policies, you could build out to more of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Build from strength.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: You take the civic cluster, you look at who's next to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Our community development friends, building from strength.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: They're taking the stronger, they're in Baltimore, they're in Philadelphia, they're all over the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Build from strength, and the strong ones are like a civic cluster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: They're not strong compared to the World Center, you know, Broadway's, but you build out from that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Build from strength to the more vulnerable neighborhoods nearby.

utterances.text: Okay, I guess I'm struggling to visualize what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: So in other words, grantees, the people we know, the IRS, the 501c3, blah, blah, blah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: When we say nonprofit, we mean not-for-profit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It doesn't mean if your parents'organ, a theater group showing at the rec center,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: No revenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: You know, I mean, that's a not-for-profit at a public facility with a cultural center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: The libraries, I know that's part of your committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We also look at embedded programs, immigrant-serving social service organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: So many of the immigrant and foreign-born organizations are cultural in our view.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We take a very broad view.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We don't just define things by the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Official 501c3 nonprofit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: Everything's nonprofit that isn't making money, okay?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: And we try to capture that, and getting to that will take more work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: It's five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: You've got a gigantic city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: We're just saying that's what, because we're Philadelphians and we've been able to come back so much, we can do stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: In another city, that's what we consider a five-city study with the five boroughs, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Seifert
utterances.text: So you have to...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: you know, Councilmember Stevens and I have been on conversations with folks in Baltimore on a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think one of the things that we realize is it's not that we're not doing some of this, it's whether or not

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: government is responding in the standardized institutional way, because, you know, I feel like in these localized communities, a lot of that like horizontal networking is happening.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But what I find and what we found and

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: if anyone else has any other questions, I'll open up to my colleagues, is that, you know, because New York City is such a big city, our government infrastructure is also not malleable.

utterances.text: So it is not flexible to certain types of change, to how we allocate money to different groups, especially for specific city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And that is an area of opportunity because I think that...

chapters.summary: Commissioner Diya Vij thanks SIAP, introduces herself, and says she will reflect on what worked, what didn't, and what DCLA is doing now to address CreateNYC's bolder ideas.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij introduces DCLA testimony on CreateNYC's 10-year review

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: First of all, just very grateful for Mark and Susan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Williams, and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm Dia Vidge, Commissioner of Cultural Affairs for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm here to testify on today's topic, What's Next for Create NYC, and I'm joined by several members of my team from the agency.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm excited to be with you here today in part because the 2017 Create NYC Cultural Plan coincided with my first stint at Cultural Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I learned so much that I still carry with me from supporting the team that built the original plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: A very small group of us then condensed those hundreds of strategies into the 2019 Action Plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, Create NYC has proven to have great impact where it set strong, broad strategies that could guide agency efforts around equity.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It fell short when it named dozens of discrete programs at varying scales and created indicators that proved hard to implement or track.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Today, I want to reflect honestly on 10 years of the Create NYC plan by examining what worked, what didn't, and what we're doing in the present day to address some of its bolder, more evergreen ideas.

utterances.text: One inescapable fact is how much the world around us changed after the plan was released.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The COVID-19 pandemic reshaped our entire city and put stresses on our cultural community we could hardly imagine in 2017.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: A new federal administration has weaponized some of the plan's foundations, radically shifting how we can approach diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Seismic changes like these require our approach and planning and policymaking to change too.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In testimony, I will talk through the five objectives outlined in the Create NYC Action Plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I want to examine what was accomplished under each objective, where we still need to focus, and what we're doing in the present day to achieve real meaningful change.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The 2019 Create NYC Action Plan was our effort to streamline the density and complexity of the original plan while still maintaining its core priorities.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I remember working with Derek Wang, my colleague next to me, and others, writing out hundreds of post-it notes and index cards to distill the original plan into something more manageable and effective.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Ultimately, we boiled the 2017 plans 180 pages into five broad objectives.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Objective one was increase equitable funding and support for culture, especially in historically underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This objective gave the agency a mandate to look into our funding practices with a lens towards equity.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Since FY18, more than $21.7 million of CDF funding has been allocated to groups in underserved neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: An admissions fee arrangement with the Met Museum announced in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: 19 provided an additional $2.8 million distributed to 175 groups across both the CDF and CIG.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The latter example shows how a broad mandate could give the agency room to respond to new opportunities, ones that couldn't be anticipated by the plan but could still be harnessed to achieve its objectives.

chapters.summary: Vij reports FY26 CDF distributed $74.3 million to 1,171 groups, up from $40 million to 950 groups in 2017, and describes multi-year support, Disability Forward Fund, Language Access Fund, Culture Pass, and IDNYC.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij details CDF and CIG funding increases and access programs

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Thanks to the budget increases for DCLA following the release of the plan, we were also able to increase funding across the CDF and target the smaller CIGs for increased operating subsidies.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The FY26 CDF distributed $74.3 million to 1,171 cultural groups.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The year the plan was released, the CDF provided just over $40 million to 950 groups.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Last year, the agency also added five members to the cultural institutions group in each of the five boroughs, the largest such expansion since the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This objective also committed to increase funding for individual artists.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: While the strategies named included grant programs under the Mayor's Office of Media and Entertainment and our own re-grant partnerships with the Borough Arts Council, this is an area of the plan that lacked much substance and consequently has lacked much impact.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It is a priority for me as Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Another strategy was exploring more flexible and multi-year support.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Starting in FY23, the agency did expand multi-year support to all eligible CDF grantees.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This year, 602 CDF groups were in a multi-year cycle, more than half of the grantee pool.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We also created new ways to educate potential grantees on the process, including a virtual application seminar.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Our recently released racial equity plan takes these strategies further with the goal of giving people back their time.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In it, we commit to conducting a review of all application and reporting requirements to simplify processes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We also commit to significantly expanding the ways we conduct outreach, something you rightly pushed for during our budget hearings earlier this year, Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Finally, this objective outlines strategies to improve cultural access for historically marginalized groups of artists, audiences, and cultural workers.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: For this, the agency launched the Create NYC Disability Forward Fund and Language Access Fund.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Together, these programs have provided more than 700 grants totaling over $7 million to organizations serving these communities.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It also calls out our partnership with the council to administer initiatives like the Cultural Immigrant Initiative and Coalition of Theaters of Color and the launch of Library's Culture Pass program.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: To date, Culture Pass has provided more than 568,000 free reservations to cultural institutions for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Another program called out in the plan, IDNYC, has provided 806,000 free cultural memberships.

chapters.summary: Vij credits former Commissioner Tom Finkelpearl, says CIG members adopted DEI plans, describes audits and pipeline programs, and notes CUNY Cultural Corps has placed over 1,100 students in paid internships.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij discusses DEI plans and CUNY Cultural Corps

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Objective two in the Create NYC Action Plan was cultivate inclusive practices in the cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I want to take a moment to recognize former Commissioner Tom Finkelpearl for heralding DEI within the cultural workforce as one of his primary policy agencies, which was not always an easy effort.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: One of the signature outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: comes with this Create NYC objective was requiring members of the CIG to adopt formal DEI plans.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Earlier this year, DCLA CIG team and myself had nearly 30 calls with members of the CIG to learn about the progress they've made on their plans in lieu of final reports.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They have done critical work from audits of hiring practices and anti-oppression trainings for staff and board to hiring senior level diversity officers and creating new pipeline programs for workers from diverse backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's clear that when DEI is prioritized consistently and over time, we see results.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We continue to see obstacles for cultural workers to advance into mid-career and leadership roles within institutions, and consequently, the Racial Equity Plan explicitly focuses goals on this part of the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The REP, Racial Equity Plan, recommits us to the CUNY Cultural Corps, which has placed over 1,100 CUNY students in paid internships at dozens of cultural institutions since it was first launched.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: While it was launched before 2017, the Cultural Corps was able to receive long-term baseline funding thanks to Create NYC.

chapters.summary: Vij describes immigration summit, commissioner office hours, Office of Nightlife, and Create in Place, which has supported over 100 creative businesses and helped Red Hook fire recovery and South of Prospect rezoning.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij reviews government connections and Create in Place

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Objective three from the action plan is to strengthen connections between the cultural sector and government.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It names new funding programs, partnerships like a summit on immigration that I was proud to organize, and office hours with the commissioner, a series of direct engagements with the commissioner launched for Create NYC that I revived when I started as commissioner earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Create NYC has also spurred the creation of the city's Office of Nightlife.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The office has opened new pathways.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: ways to support for support and collaboration between our nightlife and DIY arts venues and city government

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: from ending the March task force to increasing safety through Narcan trainings ONL has been a transformative transformative conduit between a previously overlooked sector in our city and local officials

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: since starting in 2018 the office has resolved hundreds of quality of life and venue safety cases and helped to save places like lot radio in Brooklyn from shuttering

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Another development that has reshaped our work in this area is the NYC Create in Place program.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Launched in 2024, Create in Place built on this model and put several key recommendations from Create NYC and focuses on helping cultural organizations to navigate real estate challenges.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It supports Create NYC's citywide coordination goals by working with over a dozen city agencies, including DCP, SBS, EDC, and MoM, to address real estate regulatory and other challenges.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Since its launch, the initiative has supported more than 100 creative small businesses and nonprofit arts organizations across all five boroughs and reached more than 800 people.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: When crises strike, like the fire that tore through dozens of artists and creative workspaces in Red Hook last year, Create in Place served a crucial connector between those affected and the resources that can help them recover.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In Red Hook, we secured space to triage damaged artworks and equipment and secured 75 artists and small businesses SBA loans for recovery.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Through Create in Place, we've recently been working closely with DCP to make sure that the cultural...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: community, including the 37 DCLA grantees operating in the area, is involved at the ground floor of the South of Prospect rezoning effort in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: During the pandemic, DCLA's primary focus was on emergency response and recovery.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The pandemic forged new networks, advocacy groups, and mutual aid efforts that have reshaped how the cultural sector organizes and how we share information.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Culture at Three, members of which are present in the room today, has become an indispensable forum for communicating with the sector.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I've joined the calls to meet with participants and take questions.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We've also connected other agencies like COGE and MOERJ to share information about their programs.

chapters.summary: Vij discusses AREA program's 165 units, 50,000 square feet at Brooklyn Army Terminal, and cultural space in developments like Brownsville Arts Center and People's Theater Project, but says affordability remains the most pressing challenge.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij addresses affordability crisis and affordable workspace

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The fourth objective of the action plan was to address the city's affordability crisis for the cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The Affordable Real Estate for Artists, or AREA, program was one strategy named here.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The program, supported with $10 million in capital funds, supported the creation of 165 units of affordable workspace in city-funded capital projects before it was later sunset.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We were also able to secure Art Bill 50,000 square feet in the Brooklyn Army Terminal, giving more than 100 working artists access to long-term affordable workspace.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Another strategy was to include cultural organizations and city-led development projects to provide affordable long-term space,

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: from the Brownsville Arts Center and Apartments to the People's Theater Project in Inwood to Indie Space's new facility on Manhattan's West Side to Casa Belongo in El Barrio.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This is an

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: an area that has produced exciting new opportunities for culture to be integrated into the fabric of our city in sustainable, affordable spaces.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: However, the affordability crisis remains the most pressing and layered challenge facing the field today, and it is my explicit mandate to use all levers available to DCLA to address this.

chapters.summary: Vij says the Arts Office is developing pre-K to 12 arts pathways, increased funding from $516 million in FY24 to $563 million in FY25, and DCLA supports arts education through CDF grantees, CASA, and Materials for the Arts.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij outlines arts education progress and DOE partnership

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The final objective of the action plan was to provide high-quality arts education for all NYC school students.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This is as important a commitment as it is difficult to distill into a few indicators.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The Arts Office is advancing equity by developing sequential pre-K to 12 arts pathways across all five arts disciplines, dance, music, theater, visual arts, and media arts.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They've increased arts education funding across NYC public schools and the Arts Office from $516 million in FY24 to approximately $563 million in FY25.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The City Council plays an important role in this, providing nearly $4 million in grants to 223 schools in all City Council districts for additional arts education services in the most recent school year.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: While we celebrate this work of the DOE Arts Office, we are eager to collaborate with the DOE to go farther for our students.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: DCLA supports arts education in public schools in a myriad of ways.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In FY24, 369 CDF grantees implemented projects that included an education program that served K-12 students.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: 148 organizations received CASA designation.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: from the City Council, which we're proud to administer on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And through Materials for the Arts, we are the largest provider of free arts supplies to the public school systems.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: MFTA also offers 300 free field trips to Title I schools each year.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In the CIG, the public science institutions are a pillar of science education in our schools through programs like the council-funded Urban Advantage.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: New York Hall of Science in Queens is co-located with the Universal Pre-K Center and advised on the creation of three other public education facilities in the borough.

chapters.summary: Vij says Mayor Mamdani and she doubled artist grants from $5,000 to up to $10,000, launched TDF Ticket for Teens, free Met membership for SNAP recipients, and Met Opera for All, and highlights FY27 budget of $323 million.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij announces artist grant increase and new access programs

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: As much as our city has changed in the past decade, many of the conditions and challenges have remained consistent.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The cost of living crisis was already devastating our city before the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In the 10 years since Create NYC, it's only gotten worse.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Addressing this crisis for our cultural community is my mandate and laser focus under this administration.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Just last month, Mayor Mamdani and I joined with local arts councils to announce that we are doubling grant awards to artists from $5,000 to up to $10,000, the first increase in nearly 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We were able to move forward based on conversations with working artists that we've been having and begin to address an overlooked goal of Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We've also launched partnerships like the TDF Ticket for Teens program, a free Met Museum membership for SNAP recipients, and the Met Opera Opera for All initiative to make sure that all New Yorkers can afford to participate in our city's cultural life.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In our racial equity plan, we commit to creating baseline indicators for CDF, exploring gender

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: operating and expanding multi-year support for organizations and greater data transparency.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We will soon roll out an enhanced NYC open data set that includes key information like EINs and geographic information, allowing researchers and advocates to better analyze our funding patterns.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Our record-setting budget allocation of $323 million for FY27, adopted by Mayor Mimdani and the City Council, is a step toward escaping the scarcity mindset that often forces important reforms to be put on the back burner.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This includes a $10 million cultural stability fund aimed at addressing the financial precarity our sector faces due to the affordability crisis.

chapters.summary: Vij says the plan was a valiant attempt at public engagement, DCLA has engaged over 1,000 artists and cultural workers, and will synthesize listening session findings and work with Council on district sessions.
chapters.title: Commissioner Vij commits to listening sessions and shared priorities

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The plan was big, a valiant attempt to make sure that the many New Yorkers who took the time to contribute to the process were heard and reflected in the final result.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The 1,000-plus artists, cultural workers, and residents we've engaged since I became commissioner, from

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Latine arts groups to literary orgs to artists across the boroughs to nightlife workers and so many more, have reaffirmed how important it is for us in city leadership to listen to the concerns, ideas, feedback, and community solutions.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The goal is to continue these sessions with an ongoing forum and to synthesize and share the learnings.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Being in conversations with our constituents is great, but it is only meaningful when it leads to material changes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We are committed to both.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We look forward to sharing what we learned from our listening sessions, where we've been collecting notes, transcripts, ideas, and feedback to ideas.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: identify patterns and priorities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We would also love to work together with the council to organize sessions to hear directly from constituents in your district.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Thank you for the time to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer any questions you have.
