utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And I know anecdotally that a lot of them have been hired and, you know, are finishing university and then go into a career in the arts or have a different relationship.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But shouldn't we be at a place where it's not anecdotally and we're actually tracking?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because if you can track that there was 1,100 young people that went through this program, then, like, why are we not tracking their progress?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because isn't that the point of the program?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And I believe that CUNY is starting to undergo a survey right now, a research study around what are the impacts of the internship program.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When was this program started?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So this program has been going on since 2017.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's 2026, almost nine years later, and we don't, we're not tracking these young people to see the impact of the work.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We have anecdotal data.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We have data from CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We have data from cultural organizations.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But the Department of Cultural Affairs has not done a comprehensive study.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, maybe we should, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If this is a program we're toting and saying that,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is helping with diversity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We should actually be tracking it and using it to do that work.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks what evidence shows diversity initiatives change hiring and retention; Vij says all 34 CIGs submitted equity plans and final reports, but organizations set their own goals, and board governance remains a struggle.
chapters.title: Council Member Stevens questions DEI accountability and CIG equity plans

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Would you like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What evidence shows that diversity initiative changes permanent hiring or promotional or retention for institute practices?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So do you have any evidence to show that diversity is actually happening in these institutions, like other than anecdotal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We have what has been submitted to us in the CIG reports that come every year and the CDF reports.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So we do understand the kind of practices and new initiatives that have been put in place in organizations across the city.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we rely on their hiring surveys to tell us.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How many SIGs have required to submit an equity plan, and how many submitted them, and how many providers provided the required progress reports?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: All 34.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Now there's 39, but when the reports were required, there were 34 SIGs.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: All of them submitted, reported annually, and just submitted final reports, either in writing or with meetings directly with me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Among the institutions, how many met the measurable goals due in the last reporting period, and how many missed them, and how many could not have their assessments done?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They each had, you know, they created their own goals that they measured against, and I think we saw a lot of patterns, again, around, like, the pipeline in.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: People felt very confident that they were meeting those goals.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They felt much less confident.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you just said they created their own goals?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yes, because the cultural organizations are very different, organizations to organizations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So you guys don't help with like having general goals to guide that or?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, we put out a list and we had many, many meetings and convenings to talk through like what does this look like?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But if you're an organization that has seven employees versus, I don't know, 2,000, it's different, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we do rely on them to be the experts of their own organizations to come up with that plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But we had a lot of things that were requirements around workforce development, around board development, around access to New Yorkers for their...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: work and they created their own goals based on that around disability around racial equity so

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: we learned a lot in the final reports a lot what did you learn we learned that like board governance is still something that a lot of the organization struggle with and board development in terms of a racial equity and that's all nonprofits across the board

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: but what are you guys doing specifically to help with that

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I'm six months in, so really looking forward to working on that kind of pipeline once again.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So we're not losing those mid-career workers.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We lose so many right now.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And in board governance, we're thinking about what kind of resources can we do to support organizations that are working on board development more thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a great place for DCLA to help.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think, again, that's a problem across all sectors where folks are not understanding that the importance of having a diverse board is important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And then when you look at boards, even when they are led by minorities, their board is typically not reflected of the folks that are doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I think that there's definitely work that needs to be done there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Are there any other trends that you saw from this information that they gave?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think, I mean, in a positive trend, and I was around at Cultural Affairs when we launched this initiative, and I will say it was not easy, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It took a lot of work to convince everybody that this was like a good thing to do to get a board-adopted plan, and these all had to be board-adopted.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And because of the length of time and the kind of consistency that...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: that was required of them.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They now all, many of them have like board committees on DEI.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: There's a report out in every board meeting.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: There's like some of the dance companies, it takes that long to kind of build your next generation of dancers.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And now you're seeing the result of it.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So I think what's been,

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: A pattern that's been good to see is that long-term and dedicated focus actually leads to that generational change that we're only really seeing now, I would argue.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about the action plan's living wage strategy; Vij admits it had no strategies and little impact, says wages have not improved, and Stevens urges the city to move from diagnosing problems to creating policy.
chapters.title: Council Member Stevens questions living wage strategy and cultural worker wages

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What accountability measures that you guys apply to these institutions, especially because they're making their own goals to ensure that they're not missing any of their equity goals or commitments or things like that?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, we definitely are in regular conversation with the organizations, the SIGs.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: For the CDF, it's part of the application process.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So part of the questions that you're answering are around diversity and your commitment to it and what it looks like for you and around your board composition and what governance looks like.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: That's part of how you're reviewed for grant funding.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So basically, it's just more around like if you're going to get the grant funding, like that's accountability.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like if you're not meeting these requirements, your grant could be pulled.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, and it does, it comes up quite frequently in the conversations in the peer panels.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The action plan living wage strategy lists no actions online.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has DCLA implemented it?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If so, can you identify the policy workers covered and the results?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, candidly, I think this is a

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: a huge area for growth for the agency and improvement on making an impact in this.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's definitely really important for us under this administration and under Deputy Mayor of Economic Justice, Julie Hsu.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: This is a very important area that we'll be spending a lot more time on.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Cultural workers in general and artists especially.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But you're right, there were no strategies attached to it and I think as a result it's the kind of lightest impact that came out of it and it's absolutely a priority for us.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What evidence shows whether cultural workers'wages, benefits, and job security have improved since 2017 and what impact can DCLA attribute to create NYC?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I honestly don't know that we can say that they have improved.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think we've lived through COVID, which exposed how exactly financially precarious these organizations are, how many workers had to kind of make it through that moment.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And it's a struggle, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The affordability crisis is real, and I don't know that workers are experiencing a better...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Time today than they were when this plan came out, truthfully.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think that's why we've seen a lot of cultural workers unionize over the past 10 years, which is amazing, but it is absolutely an area that needs to be deeper, deeply considered.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I just want to say I don't think we should be at a point where we're still blaming Culver for stuff.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, I think that we're past that, and I think...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, yes, I know we've been talking about affordable city, but I think we need to move from, like, this is what the problem is and actually fix it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And we just can't keep saying we want an affordable city.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We have to start to create policy that drives that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you, Deputy Speaker, for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that's it is all.

chapters.summary: Louis asks how many affordable cultural spaces CreateNYC helped create or preserve since 2017; Vij cites 165 artist workspace units but says she does not know how many were lost, and says an all-of-government plan is coming soon.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis asks about affordable cultural space created and lost

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I just have a quick question.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I know we all are very much aware of how many vacancies we see in storefronts across the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: That includes nonprofits and cultural spaces.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: So I wanted to know how many affordable cultural spaces has Create NYC helped create or preserve since 2017?

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I know you're only six months in, but would love if you could expound on that and how many were lost over the same period of time.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Through Create NYC, DCLA built and secured 165 units of affordable space, workspace for artists in particular.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I am not sure how much was lost in that time period.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think the social impact of the arts study that's coming out does a very good job at showing how many

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: showing that kind of difference of nonprofits in the city 10 years ago from now.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Okay, but it would be good to know if we could have a follow-up on that.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, it's a big, we didn't lose

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: All of the ones that Department of Cultural Affairs developed are still running, up and running.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But Space Works was functioning in the beginning of the plan and has since sunsetted.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So that's also why the Affordable Real Estate for Artists program kind of sunsetted as well.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But affordable space and affordable workspace for artists is also a really big priority for us.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we're really looking into taking an all-of-government approach to understand how we do this.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Do you guys have an actual plan for that?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's coming soon.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair asks for the three most consequential achievements since 2017; Vij cites deep public engagement, funding reforms targeting under-resourced neighborhoods, and DEI work becoming core to DCLA.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks Commissioner Vij for CreateNYC's top achievements

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just some overall questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What are Create New York City's three most consequential achievements since 2017 and what evidence demonstrates their impact?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I would say, well, I really do think that the plan kind of transformed the way DCLA worked in terms of that really deep public engagement, having those office hours of the commissioners, the town halls, the borough workshops, the

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: public poll, it just like transformed, really opened the doors between DCLA and the people that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And that has actually been transformative, that kind of accountability direct to...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: constituent.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I would say the funding transformations have been really significant.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The CDF reforms and the way that we think about SIAP funding or, you know, adding additional funds to target neighborhoods that are under-resourced.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And then also like the Disability Forward Fund, the Language Access Fund, and just in general, the cultural plan allowed the Department of Cultural Affairs to really transform its argument away from just the economic

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: argument into that social impact neighborhood level justification for what we do, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: That we started to be able to say with proof that arts and culture have these like really meaningful and profound impacts on the social well-being of people.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So we're able to start

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: to move resources more on that neighborhood level and less only geared towards what art can do for tourism.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So in a lot of ways, it totally transformed how we think about our work and then how we're able to build policies outside of that.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And then I would say the DEI work was really significant and transformative.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And it is not something that before the Create NYC plan was part of this agency's purview.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And now it really is kind of core to how we work with the cultural organizations.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: That it's a really big part of how they kind of have to be accountable to the city.

chapters.summary: Vij says living wages for cultural workers and artists remain unfulfilled, arts education needs more work with DOE, and DCLA alone cannot change conditions without an all-of-government approach.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks which CreateNYC commitments remain unfulfilled

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Which major commitments remain unfulfilled?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think the ones that we were just talking about in terms of living wages for cultural workers and artists.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think there was, I do think that the piece of the plan, that was the lightest piece of the plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Workers and artists are still struggling against this affordability crisis today.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: That's something we absolutely have to address.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think we have a lot of work to do with our colleagues in the DOE to continue to move arts education forward and to think about maybe new or deeper ways that the cultural field can collaborate with schools, although they do a lot already.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And in general, just the kind of all of government approach.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think what we learned from the plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's like DCLA alone, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The policies that come out of our office are not going to wholesale change the conditions for workers in New York City that will positively impact.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Cultural workers and artists, that that's an all of government approach.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So I think also in these areas where we're looking into that kind of inner city coordination, there's a lot more there to think about how culture is at the table across city government.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's not just DCLA holding it, but all of us together holding that work and that cultural inclusion is part of other agencies'priorities.

chapters.summary: Vij says the listening tour has reached all five boroughs and 15 sessions, with affordable space as the biggest issue, and says DCLA is synthesizing findings but has not determined the reporting format.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about listening tour findings and written accounting

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The committee understands that the commissioner, as you also mentioned, has been on a listening tour getting feedback from the cultural community about, among other things, the city's cultural plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What has DCLA learned from that tour?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then in connection with a potential update of the plan, will DCLA provide a full written accounting showing what from existing plan was completed, modified, abandoned, or never attempted?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Well, the listening tour has been great so far.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: After this week, we're going to Staten Island this week.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We would have been to all five boroughs, 15 of them total.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we've learned, I think, like, to no one's surprise, the biggest issue everyone's facing is access to affordable space and then being able to stay in space.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So for artists, that's workspace.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: For cultural organizations, it's their anchor spaces in their neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We're learning about how difficult it is to have consistent support for artists and workers around like

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I mean, yeah, space and affordability, it's really, really big.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And for artists, it's also about health insurance and access to just the kind of basics to make a great quality life here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And in terms of reporting, we are currently, all of these listening sessions, we transcribe them, we take notes, we're synthesizing all of that information and we'll put out those findings.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We're still determining what that will look like and are happy to work with you as we...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Determine that.

chapters.summary: Chair asks who tracks implementation; Derek Wang says the plan is updated biannually and a team effort, but Chair notes CreateNYC is not his only responsibility and asks if staff are assigned specifically.
chapters.title: Chair Williams questions who tracks CreateNYC implementation and staffing

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, the charter makes DCLA responsible for implementing and overseeing the plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Who currently tracks implementation across agencies and what staff and budget support that work?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, we report out through our Create NYC website, of course, through the MMR, and Derek actually holds a lot of the work for the agency, so I'll let you put some more color onto that.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: Yeah, so the plan is updated biannually.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: So every two years, we upload the latest action plan item updates on our main website.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: And then the key indicator, we also just updated the website as well.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: So you could see exactly what we've accomplished throughout the years.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And who tracks that?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you read?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Who tracks that?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Who tracks that work?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So who updates?

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: It's a team effort.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: It's commission unit, you know, the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: We all work together to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So is there a specific staff assigned to advance Create NYC or is it?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's a hodgepodge of people having to take on this task in addition to all their other responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because, like, what is your title?

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: I'm special projects manager, so I did work with Dia on the creation of.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But, like, Create NYC isn't your only thing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: No, Derek is in the CIG unit.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But I will say, like, over these 10 years, so much of the Create NYC plan has been institutionalized, and so much of its work comes out of every single unit.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: It's kind of a lens that everyone takes to approach their work.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So like the CDF reforms, that lives within the CDF unit, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And like how to think about equitable funding or percent for art when they're commissioning artists.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: What does equity look like geographically?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Also who the artists are, what community engagement is.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So at this point, it really is like spread out as part of everybody's job.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And the data tracking is...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: also a team effort and Derek kind of brings it all together and spearheads it for us.

chapters.summary: Chair says reports were hard to find online and asks if 2023 and 2025 reports were submitted to mayor and speaker; Vij promises to send them, and Wang says FY23-FY26 data was uploaded over the weekend.
chapters.title: Chair Williams presses DCLA on missing biennial reports and key indicator data

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I know you mentioned that you publish the progress reports that are due every two years after submission of the original plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But we had trouble actually finding some of those reports online.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know and get clarity if you submitted the reports for 2023 and 2025 cycles to both the mayor and the speaker.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We have absolutely put them on the website and published them, but we will look in to make sure that we are fully in compliance and moving forward we'll be definitely submitting them to the mayor and speaker.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's supposed to be submitted to the mayor and the speaker, correct?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is that what the charter?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, the charter stipulates that it's supposed to be submitted to both the mayor and the speaker.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I don't think we received it.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Okay, well, we will definitely send them to you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The Create NYC Key Indicators page promises updates at the close of each fiscal year, but its tables generally stop at FY 2022.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So where subsequent years data collected but not published or not collected, again, who is responsible and when will the missing data be published?

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: Yeah, as I've said before, during the weekend, we uploaded some new numbers.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: So you'll find numbers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's so convenient because you knew you were coming to the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: You'll find numbers from FY23 to FY26.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Not acceptable, but we appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's why hearings are important.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It holds people accountable.

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: I would also say, I mean.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because I don't know if we had this hearing, if you would have rushed to put those things online.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm just saying.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But we appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Chair asks who serves on the commission and when it last met; Vij says DCLA is appointing new members and current members are still in their seats, but no new appointments since administration change.
chapters.title: Chair Williams questions Cultural Affairs Advisory Commission roster and meetings

utterances.speaker: Derek Wang
utterances.text: I would say just during the different administration, there's also a lot of staff turnover as well.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, I did read the article with the former commissioner talking about how politics definitely get in the way of a lot of these plans.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But I will also just follow that up to say that we are really committed to data transparency and put that in our racial equity plan.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We talk about missing data.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: DCLA's Cultural Affairs Advisory Commission webpage still lists former officeholders as ex-officio members and several other members on the public roster who appear to no longer be involved.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So who currently serves on the commission?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What are their appointment and term dates?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And when did the commission last meet?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We're currently in the process of appointing new members to that commission to be up and running in the next month or so.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, so can you help us understand why the information is inaccurate online?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I don't know that they are officially not serving.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They are still in their seats.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We just have not appointed new members since the administration change.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And again, a section in the charter, 2505, assigns the commission policy coordination and research functions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What create NYC findings are?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: recommendations did the commission produce and what action did DCLA take in response?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The commission was very involved.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They not only in giving their own feedback, but in organizing various public engagements with their own communities to have input into the plan from like the first meetings through the final reports.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So it's hard to point to exactly the areas where they

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: contributed, but their thinking, ideas, and desires are kind of all over the plan.

chapters.summary: Chair asks how DCLA identifies underserved communities; Vij says the racial equity plan will establish baseline metrics, disability community needs more attention, and disparities have widened even as some neighborhoods became civic clusters.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks which communities remain least served by cultural funding

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Which communities remain least served by city cultural funding?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How does DCLA identify them?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And how much have those disparities narrowed since 2017?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, part of the racial equity plan we just released, we have committed to establishing baseline metrics so that we can start really analyzing that information ourselves moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I would say for sure the disability community was such a priority when we were making this plan and will be again, but that is definitely an area that needs more attention from us.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And then I think as you heard from Social Impact of the Arts, there are definitely some great neighborhood trends that can be pulled from the past 10 years around those civic clusters in particular and how more neighborhoods have

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: become civic clusters, so like more resilient, more dense in cultural life, but there has also been a widening of disparities.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So that is absolutely something that needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, it would be helpful if, like, the agency itself, like, had a cadre of communities that you can point to, you know, because I think that would demonstrate that you're actually making assessments.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I'm not saying that you aren't, but you didn't really list, like, specific communities that I'm sure, like, anecdotally we could say.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know where you're funding.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know where the organizations are doing their work.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know that I just looked at the list of all the organizations receiving CDF funding.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I feel like even from the data that you currently collect, I would hope that there is an assessment on what communities are underserved, even boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, I know Queens loves to say oftentimes that we don't get our fair share of cultural funding.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So and that's just a whole borough.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I feel like.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: A whole borough is as large as a city as we just described.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So like really getting more granular into like neighborhood communities, it would be interesting to kind of have a better sense from DCLA, like your focus.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cause that I think would make me feel more comfortable that you're actually like looking at what communities are truly underserved by cultural funding versus this sort of,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: macro approach.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Unless you have more information, I'm willing to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like you do.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: We are, I mean, I said already, like, we are spending this year, as we committed in our racial equity plan, to really do that deep dive and establish those

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: metrics for ourselves to be able to provide to you that more granular information to hold ourselves accountable to moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we know where we fund, but I do kind of think that's the tip of the iceberg, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: There's so much more we need to understand in order to know the depth of funding, the consistency of that investment, and what the impacts of that are beyond just organization to organization.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So we are very much looking into this and understanding what baseline data we should build to...

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Track over time, which I do think is probably something that the original cultural plan could have done a little bit better, is put those in from the beginning so that we're able to track ourselves internally and understand the impact of our work more clearly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you have a timeline for that work?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: End of 2027.

chapters.summary: Chair asks if the plan changes who receives funding; Vij says it makes process commitments, including general operating support, multi-year support, streamlined applications, multilingual outreach, and deeper relationships with borough arts councils.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks if racial equity plan changes funding allocations

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: FY 2027 is our goal.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Does DCLA's revised racial equity plan commit to changing who receives funding, or does it just make process commitments or maybe metric commitments to assess?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If so, what allocation targets and deadlines apply?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, we do make process.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: recommendations and goals for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The processes are peer reviewed, so we don't have in, you know, we won't say that an outcome, we won't predict an outcome for the panel,

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: but we'd have put forward a series of process changes that we hope to look into based on public feedback and what we know is just is more equitable looking into general operating support, looking into rethinking multi-year and what that looks like for our organizations.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And again, like streamlining our application processes and doing much more outreach and multilingual outreach to get more

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: organizations in the door and also increasing our depth of relationship with the borough arts councils, which will help us reach not only individual artists, but also those grassroots arts organizations that are

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: smaller than what DCLA would award to on their own.

chapters.summary: Vij cites IDNYC's 805,000 memberships and Culture Pass's 560,000 reservations as access gains, and says the Disability Forward Fund has provided about 600 grants totaling over $6 million.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about cultural participation and disability gains

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What evidence shows increased cultural participation among residents of historically underserved neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, we have, we do collect this information from the CIG, which we can share afterwards, but I thought that the numbers

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: around cultural access that came out of the cultural plan were like pretty staggering, like the IDNYC 800 plus thousand memberships, the culture pass over 150,000.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Where's Culture Pass?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Oh, gosh.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Over 560,000 passes reserved to dates of Culture Pass.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And Culture Pass, of course, is through the library.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So those are all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And same with IDNYC.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Those are all New York City residents, 805,000 of them that received one-year memberships at at least one cultural organization.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So that is like a dramatic shift in access.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What measurable gains have disabled artists and cultural workers made in employment, funding, and leadership, not only physical access to facilities?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: The Disability Forward Fund is given to CDF applicants, and same with the Language Access Fund.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And so to date, there's been about 600 grants totaling over $6 million for that, and that's access, but that's also

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: funding for disabled artists to be able to perform or present their work in spaces or to do outreach to disabled communities.

chapters.summary: Chair asks if the charter-mandated interagency coordination plan exists; Vij points to Create in Place and a monthly interagency task force, but Chair says the plan sounds more comprehensive and Vij concedes it is fair to say DCLA does not have it.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about interagency coordination plan and cultural infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So the charter calls for an interagency coordination plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Was that plan created?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is it written?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Are you able to share it?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I believe that the response to that plan was really can be found in Create in Place, this newish program that was launched in 2024 that

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: specifically responds to cultural organizations of all sizes, particularly very small ones that are at risk of losing.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: their space.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And there is a really large interagency task force that meets monthly around issues of space, real estate, and cultural access.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And I'm happy to share more information about that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I think, I mean, I don't have like the charter language in front of me, but I think it was more comprehensive than like

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: a create in place program.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It was more so around like how do you embed cultural arts within all the various city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So yeah, DCLA was supposed to create a interagency coordination plan around that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I don't, sounds like maybe you don't have it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I think that's fair to say.

chapters.summary: Chair says she had to force arts into her neighborhood plan; Vij agrees and cites Gowanus affordable artist studios and South of Prospect rezoning as models for early cultural inclusion.
chapters.title: Chair Williams and Commissioner Vij discuss embedding culture in neighborhood planning

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What formal process ensures cultural infrastructure is considered in housing, economic development, and neighborhood planning decisions?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Where has that process changed outcomes?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think this just goes back to some of the interagency coordination plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I can think about my neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We had to force arts and culture into the conversation, and I think this is an opportunity for sister agencies to better collaborate with one another.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And it's been a big focus of all of my meetings with other agencies and are really kind of putting a lot of work internally into how we do that.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So it's not advocates needing to spend all of their time advocating on a neighborhood by neighborhood level.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And when rezonings come out, I think what we see in.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Gowanus is so amazing.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I just went to their open studios this week to see affordable artist studios built in to all new developments as a requirement and the community benefits agreements they were able to negotiate is a very good model for us moving forward and create in place does a lot of this

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: work so now we're working in the south south of prospect rezoning very early on to get cultural organizations in the door from the beginning in order to do a lot of that that work of man you know cultural inclusion

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What cross-agency commitments has DCLA been able to advance?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What specific governance changes would resolve, I think, the many barriers when I speak to different cultural institutions?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And not even just cultural institutions, even bids.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, bids produce art.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And a lot of times they share frustrations around how DOT manages their, what is it?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Their plazas that they often have to maintain.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But it's in partnership with DOT as almost like a contractor.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I mean, I think the amazing thing about this city is that there is art all over city government.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And I also think that is the opportunity for us to come together to streamline how we work and make it.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Consistent for organizations and individuals trying to access from site to site.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And it is something that we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: internally to what are the best ways to kind of start to think about these processes.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But our public art team meets with the DOT arts and parks arts teams quite regularly and are in touch and are kind of navigate that on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But similarly, I think there's an opportunity to go one notch further and streamline as policy.

chapters.summary: Chair asks what standard measures high-quality arts education; Vij says that is a DOE question but DCLA meets with the chancellor and DOE Arts frequently, and Chair notes the chancellor did not answer a reporter's question on arts commitments.
chapters.title: Chair Williams questions DCLA on arts education standards and DOE relationship

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What standard does DCLA and New York City Public Schools use to assess the goal of high-quality arts education for every public school student?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And how has arts education access gaps between affluent and historically underserved school communities changed since 2017?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So that is, of course, a question for our colleagues at the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Our relationship to schools is through funding cultural organizations that do programs after school and school, or more recently are co-locating or working as providers themselves, which is very exciting.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But the NYCPS Arts Office is advancing equity, right?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: They're developing sequential pre-K to 12 art pathways.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And are increasing system-wide investment in arts education from FY 2014, that was $516 million, and FY 2025, that was $563 million.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So they have been increasing their funding and digging more deeply into creating sequential arts education.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But again, that is a question for our colleagues in the DOE around assessment.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, what is that relationship?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because I know you guys, like you created the plan as in DCLA and like you even mentioned in your testimony that, you know, one of the final objectives was to provide high quality arts education for all New York City school students.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I know that it's New York City public schools that essentially has to administer that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But you all are within like New York City government.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I view it like as sister brother agencies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What is your relationship and engagement?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, is there regular meetings?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, how are you working with New York City public schools?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because I feel like though that information, of course, should rest with them, because you all created the plan, I think that...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think it should give you some level of hierarchy to hold various other agencies accountable for delivering on what was the plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just it would be helpful to understand, like, what is DCLA's relationship with New York City public schools in advancing this objective?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I mean, I met with the chancellor a few times and I meet with the head of the DOE Arts pretty

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: frequently and are ramping up our collaborations together for both what we do with our cultural organizations, but also how we can be more collaborative or helpful.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: or supportive in arts ed in public schools.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So that is definitely something that is happening between us.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: But you're right that the arts education in public schools is held by the DOE and they are state standards.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: So we are a little bit removed from that, but our relationship is strong.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, we also have mayoral control, so the administration does wield a ton of power to sort of make certain decisions around school policy, even within the CEC board.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, the mayor has share positions on the CEC board, so I think that there's still an opportunity if the administration as a whole is committed to it, that they do have some certain inherent powers by way of, like, mayoral control to

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: make decisions within New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we are, of course, committed to increasing the quality of arts education in public schools.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, when I was at the press conference, a reporter had asked, you were there too, a reporter had asked what the commitment was for arts and culture in New York City public schools, and the chancellor did not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I love Chancellor Samuels, but he did not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I think it still is a big question around how New York City public schools is ensuring arts education, supporting arts teachers and people who are providing services outside of what New York City public schools is providing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I think that is a very audacious place for you all to be in because did not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think based off of.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: what I'm hearing is still is a big concern for many schools and many principals trying to provide robust arts education to their students and not really having the resources to do it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So, especially in certain schools.

chapters.summary: Chair asks what funding, institutional, or priority changes DCLA will propose; Vij says DCLA is gathering feedback and will share measurable priorities, but is not sure it will be a full-blown plan.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks what DCLA will propose for CreateNYC's original vision

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, the last question is what changes to

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: funding allocations, institutional arrangements, or city priorities, is DCLA prepared to propose to fulfill Create NYC's original vision?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Yeah, well, yes, we are in the process of doing this, these public engagements and collecting information and feedback from folks all over the city, different parts of the field, and also just New Yorkers that are

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: participating in the cultural life to distill those top priorities and using lessons learned from that first plan really come up with.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: What is like measurable priorities for us to implement for this administration.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, and in that vein, will the next plan include dedicated funding, name agency responsibilities, measurable targets, enforceable deadlines?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If not, how will it avoid repeating all the same accountability gaps?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then lastly, like from a visionary perspective, what concrete outcomes should New Yorkers expect by 2030?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And when and where will DCLA publish progress against those commitments?

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Well, we are certainly committed to releasing our findings and priorities from that.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: Sure that that will be a full-blown plan, but it will be

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: direction that the public can see that they have participated in and put forth for us.

utterances.speaker: Diya Vij
utterances.text: And we are, you know, we'll be sharing that in the upcoming months with more detail.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

chapters.summary: Arden Armbruster introduces herself as IBO lead budget and policy analyst, explains IBO's mission, and says the report series examines CDF grantees to inform CreateNYC's future.
chapters.title: Arden Armbruster introduces IBO's CDF report series

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Williams and members of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: My name is Arden Armbruster, and I'm a lead budget and policy analyst at the New York City Independent Budget Office, IBO.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO is a government agency whose mission is to enhance understanding of New York City's budget, public policy, and economy through independent analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We appreciate the opportunity to testify at today's hearing on the city's cultural plan, Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The first objective of the Create NYC Action Plan is to increase equitable funding and support for culture, especially in historically underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Given that the vast majority of cultural organizations that receive support from DCLA do so through the CDF grant program, the CDF has been a key lever in DCLA's ability to realize the goals of Create NYC and this first objective in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Today, IBO will share top-level findings from two reports in a forthcoming series about CDF grantees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The first report was published today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: This series is intended to support the council, the administration, and the cultural sector in understanding the current

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: state of the CDF as the city considers the future of Create NYC and cultural policy in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: If members of the committee are interested in discussing the report in more detail, IBO can coordinate with your staff for a walkthrough of the findings.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says half of CDF grantees have budgets under $500,000 and two or fewer full-time employees, two-thirds serve historically underserved communities, and the smallest grantees receive half their revenue from government.
chapters.title: IBO finds CDF grantees are small, underserved-focused, and government-reliant

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO used application and award data from the fiscal year 2025 grant cycle to understand characteristics of CDF grantees, how large they are,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: how reliant they are on government funding, which communities they serve, where they're based, and where they plan CDF programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO found that the CDF funds many small nonprofits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Half of grantees had budgets under half a million dollars and two or fewer full-time employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Two-thirds of grantees serve the historically underserved communities discussed in Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Specifically, these are grantees whose mission's name and or whose proposed CDF projects intentionally serve people of color, people with disabilities, and people whose primary language is not English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Grantees serving people of color and or people whose primary language is not English had smaller budgets on average than grantees that did not indicate serving these communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO also found that the smaller the grantee was, the more reliant they tended to be on government funding, particularly from city sources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The smallest grantees, with budgets under $100,000, received half of their revenue from the government, whereas the largest CDF grantees, with budgets of $3 million or more, received around 10% of their funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: from government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: City funds, largely from the CDF, were the largest source of government funding for grantees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Substantial city support for small grantees also means that changes at the city level can be especially impactful for these grantees, many of which also serve underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Small grantees may also be more susceptible to affordability concerns and may struggle to navigate government processes with limited staff capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: This speaks to the action plan objectives to address the affordability crisis and strengthen the connections between the cultural sector and government.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says 60% of grantees are based in Manhattan and 63% of funding goes to them, 74% of grantees planned programs in Manhattan, and planned CDF programs are not equitably distributed across boroughs.
chapters.title: IBO reports geographic inequities in CDF grantee locations and programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Another aim of Create NYC is to improve cultural access, one component of which is geographic proximity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Because grantees provide programs at their headquarters and across the city, IBO looked at both where grantees are based and where they plan CDF programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO found that 60% of grantees were based in Manhattan and 63% of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Percent of funding went to those grantees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: While Manhattan-based organizations do plan CDF programs outside of Manhattan, they do not do so at higher rates than grantees based in some of the other boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: For example, 43% of Manhattan grantees plan CDF programs outside of Manhattan, while 48% of Brooklyn grantees plan CDF programs outside of Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Additionally, some grantees from outside of Manhattan plan programs in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Across all grantees, 74% planned CDF programs in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Grantees' planned programs may differ for where programs ultimately occurred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO is currently analyzing CDF program location data as part of this series.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Still, these initial findings suggest that planned CDF programs are not equitably distributed across the five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says CDF grantees are responsive to underserved communities but small and government-reliant, so city policies have outsized impact; IBO will publish more reports and host a webinar on Thursday.
chapters.title: IBO summarizes implications and announces upcoming reports and webinar

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: In summary, because most cultural organizations receiving DCLA support do so through the CDF,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Create NYC's goals to improve cultural equity and access hinge on CDF grantees and the programs they provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO found that many of the nonprofits funded by the CDF are responsive to underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: But these same grantees are often small and reliant on government funding for a considerable portion of their income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: This means that city policies can have an outsized impact on them, positively and negatively, a dynamic with direct implications for the city's ability to meet any cultural equity goals it sets in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO encourages anyone interested in these findings to visit our website to read the next report in this series.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Sign up for IBO's newsletter and follow us on social media to be notified when the next reports are published.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We are also hosting a webinar on cultural policy and public administration this Thursday at 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: With details and registration on our website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify today, and I'm happy to take any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So I will say one major difference is our report is looking specifically at the CDF.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The Local Law 15 reports that I have seen online are sort of PDFs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: There's some text at the top and then tables of sort of each individual organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: That's quite different from the way we approached this analysis, which is really like a statistical analysis looking at trends within the grantees themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: One thing that I like to say when I talk about my work is it can be really difficult to like come to some kind of conclusion when you're just looking at mountains and mountains of data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And so it can be hard to know looking at a table of sort of the grantee name, where they're based and how much money they got, any of these kinds of trends, geographic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: funding levels, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So what we've done in this report is really try to break out those trends, not only by funding amounts and geographies, but other characteristics, like some of the demographic characteristics that are specified in Local Law 15

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: around organizations that serve specifically people of color, people with disabilities, and immigrants.

chapters.summary: Armbruster emphasizes EINs in open data for targeted planning, geographic distribution of grantees and programs, and the limited capacity of small organizations that serve underserved communities.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks IBO what Council should keep in mind for future cultural policy

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if the council were to pass legislation requiring another cultural plan or other cultural policies, what do you think would be most important for us to keep in mind from your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: I think actually one thing that was coming to mind with the commissioner's testimony was it was very exciting to hear that EINs are going to be included in open data moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The laughter is because I really love EINs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: But I mentioned that because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: For a couple of reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: One, it allows for sort of more targeted planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: It allows us to connect information about the grantees to other public sources of information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And to the point earlier about sort of intergovernmental collaboration, the biggest users of open data are actually other government employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So I have used the DCLA open data data sets before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: I would say data access and transparency is certainly something that IBO is always excited about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The other

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: There are a couple of things I would mention are two things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So one is the geographic distribution of grantees and programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So I mentioned that 43% of Manhattan-based organizations were planning programs outside of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: That means that 57% of Manhattan grantees were not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And because 60% of the grantees are based in Manhattan, that sort of inevitably skews programming toward Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And there are a lot of cultural institutions in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: There's a lot of cultural infrastructure in Manhattan, enough so that organizations in other boroughs are coming into Manhattan to produce their CDF programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The flip side of that is the organizations outside of Manhattan, so for example, the Bronx, 70% of CDF grantees in the Bronx are only planned CDF programs in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So there's an opportunity there if the council and the administration are interested in rethinking the geographic distribution of programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We do now have a little bit more information about how different grantees based in different places plan their CDF programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And then the other thing I would just say quickly is about grantee size.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: A lot of these grantees are very small organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Half of them have two or fewer full-time employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And many of the organizations that serve the underserved communities that the council and the administration are interested in expanding access to are also very small.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: small organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So any plan around improving those sort of questions of access will involve small organizations and therefore should

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: be mindful of the limited capacity and ability to navigate complex government processes that they have.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.
