chapters.summary: Gregorio Mayers, founder of Panama 507 Roundtable, shares his personal story of Panamanian music, traces reggaeton's Afro-Caribbean roots, and urges passage of Resolution 625 while recommending inclusion of Reggae Sam.
chapters.title: Gregorio Mayers testifies for Resolution 625 on Reggaeton Heritage Month

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to speak here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Happy congratulations on your doctorate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Council Member Farrah Lewis and the other members of the City Council who are certainly online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: My name is Gregorio Mayers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I'm the founder and CEO of Panama 507 Roundtable Group, a public policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Think Tank advanced in the civic, cultural, and economic interests of Panamanian community in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I'm here to encourage you to pass Resolution 625 and declare October Reggaeton Heritage Month in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I come to this as a personal story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I grew up in the country of Panama.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: In a generation shaped by black music, Latino music.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: In our community, that music arrived from everywhere, from James Brown and the Jackson 5 when they visited Panama, to Bob Marley's music playing in our homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: These were part of the Panamanian story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Our parents carried that sound with them, and it became part of how we understood ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Then the younger generation took what they heard from the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: and made it their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: They put their own experiences into the words and they translated these words into Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: That is how African American rhythm and Caribbean rhythm inherited from our parents became voice of our own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: That personal story also is part of a larger story, which the resolution puts into public record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: As the resolution recites, reggaeton began in the Afro-Caribbean community in Panama, among descendants of migrant workers who built the canal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: They came about late 1895, 1900.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Canal was built to finish in 1914.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: 80,000 came from the Caribbean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: In the early 80s, 1980s, artists in that community, including Renato El General, meaning the general, began adapting Jamaican dancehall into Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: That is reggae en español, the foundation of what the world now calls reggaeton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: It gave...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: A community that faced discrimination and marginalization, a way to speak its identity out loud.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: And New York is part of this story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: The resolution notes that in 1985, El General moved to Brooklyn and enrolled at Medgar Evers College, and that he worked with the local Caribbean producers and immersed himself in the city's dance hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: and hip-hop scenes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Well, interested enough, I was a freshman that same year at the same institution, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: He was, I guess, in the performing arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I went on to law school afterwards, but same year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Panama 507 Roundtable knows what it means to bring history to the open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: We led the community effort to secure the Little Panama Way street co-naming, and we did it by working directly with the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: On September 24th, we unveiled Little Panama Way on Franklin Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Our community, cultural leaders, elected officials stood together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: We're grateful to the council that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: That participated and with a partnership with Crystal Hudson, which was her district, Sandy Nurse, who was born in Panama, right in my same community, and Pharrell Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: I also asked the council to reconsider two Panamanian artists in its legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: First, Renato Adler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Which you do have him on there, a Panamanian reggaeton legend and one of the most influential of that era for the younger generation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Second, Reggae Sam, who I recommend the council includes as reggaeton artist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Reggae Sam is also the artist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: Who released the song for Little Panama Way, Streetway, co-naming Franklin Avenue, which again was led by Councilmember Crystal Hudson,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: The Panamanian-born Sandy Nurse and Farrah Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: This is a really exciting time that we are here doing this, and it's really historic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: The New York Times has quoted that reggaeton did start in Panama as well, in New York Times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: So this month, reggaeton, we would love to have it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: This history passed on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: It will be an honor for artists and musicians and producers behind this music scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: It will encourage programming that tells the story, including the Afro-Panamanian pioneers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: And it will teach each new generations that Panama, Puerto Rico, and New York built something that now reaches every corner of the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers
utterances.text: On behalf of the 55,000 Panamanians who are registered voters living in the five boroughs, I ask that you recognize this legacy and to pass this resolution this October as we culminate Hispanic Heritage Month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gregorio Mayers

chapters.summary: Mauricio Delfin of the Culture and Arts Policy Institute argues CreateNYC conflated an agency plan with a sector-wide agenda, and proposes a DCLA capacity-building plan plus a shared cultural policy agenda with shared indicators and reporting.
chapters.title: Mauricio Delfin proposes separating DCLA capacity plan from shared cultural agenda

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Good morning, Deputy Speaker Williams and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: My name is Mauricio Delfin, and I co-direct the Culture and Arts Policy Institute with Gonzalo Casals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: My testimony continues the testimonies on Create NYC and makes one argument.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The city's next step regarding cultural plans should be to separate what DCLA can deliver on its own from what many actors must agree on and deliver together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Create NYC, the city's first legally mandated cultural plan, was shaped by more than 188,000 New Yorkers and addressed the full range of the city's cultural life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Yet DCLA was its primary implementer and sole reporter, and those reports stopped being published after 2019, as we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The lesson from Create NYC, we believe, is that an agency plan and a sector-wide agenda are different instruments, and it was asked to be both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: An agency plan depends on one agency's budget, staff, and capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: A sector-wide agenda depends on many actors, DCLA and other city agencies, the council, nonprofit and civic organizations, philanthropy, the private sector, partners in education and health, artists, and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So when DCLA reporting stopped, no other actor had the mandate or data to keep the work visible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: We therefore propose that the city develop two instruments, one for each role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: One, a capacity building plan for DCLA, and two, a shared agenda for cultural policy in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The capacity building plan should begin with an assessment of DCLA today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: with civic participation built in, how the agency collects data, evaluates its programs, and reports to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The assessment would identify the agency's capacity gaps and tell the council what to fund to close them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: That capacity will let the agency evaluate the programs it funds today, so funding decisions rest on evidence of what works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: A shared agenda for cultural policy convened by DCLA and the Council is a set of policy priorities these actors agree on, with mechanisms to carry them out, such as shared indicators and regular public reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: It also requires standing spaces for them to meet, divide responsibilities, and review progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Each actor would be accountable for its part, and reporting would show who is delivering so the work continues when what falters or an administration changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: We urge the committee to require DCLA to develop a capacity building plan starting with an assessment of its current capacity and to support a shared agenda for cultural policy in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gonzalo Casals says CreateNYC rested on an agency with 0.25% of the city budget, and proposes embedding culture in health, education, and social services, citing Massachusetts cultural prescriptions and the public artists in residence program.
chapters.title: Gonzalo Casals argues for culture as public infrastructure across city government

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Buenas tardes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: I appreciate the Latino panel here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker Williams and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: My name is Gonzalo Casals, and I'm co-director of the Culture and Arts Policy Institute, along with Mauricio.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Mauricio proposed a shared agenda for cultural policy, and I wanted to speak about his purpose, placing culture at the core of every aspect of civic life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Culture's public impact is well documented, as our friend Saya mentioned, and agencies across the city government own it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Yet, CRIENYC rested only on an agency with about 0.25% of the city budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: A new agenda that treats culture as public infrastructure, owed to every neighborhood, like parks, schools, and libraries, will do three things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: First, it builds cultural impact into services the city already provides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: In Massachusetts, doctors and social workers prescribe cultural programs the way they refer patients to a nutritionist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Providers wrote more than 1,900 prescriptions in four years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: New York's public hospitals could do the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Second, it builds understanding and with it advocates across city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Since 2015, the city's public artists in residency program has embedded 24 artists in 15 agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: But it remains a residency, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Great program, but it's not policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: As a citywide policy, it would bring city workers, artists, cultural workers together in every agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: multiplying innovation, improving services, and strengthening cultural advocates, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The difference of, you know, just an artist doing a project and just thinking policy-wise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And third, it brings new funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: When culture serves an agency mission, that agency has a reason to pay for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Massachusetts designed its programs to pay cultural organizations for the health benefits they provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Here, that means health, education, and social services dollars working for culture as new funds, not a share of the ECLA's budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: According to our friends at IBO, in fiscal year 2022, more than 2,000 city agencies and offices beyond DCLA and the public libraries paid cultural nonprofits at least $89 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: That is double the $39 million more than the DCLA awarded in competitive grants that year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The city does not track that spending, and no plans connect that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: As a shared agenda would put that money to work on purpose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The city would know what it spends on culture and what that spending achieves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Agencies would buy cultural services toward priorities they set together rather than contract by contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Cultural organizations would gain a public market beyond this LA they can plan around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And New Yorkers would find culture built into the services they few expect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Arts-based diversion programs instead of detention, creative aging and standards to service to combat isolation, and aborts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: elections outreach to new voters through cultural organizations to state a few.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Create NYC asked one agency to carry the city's cultural life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: What comes next should ask the whole city to carry it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair asks about the difference; Delfin says the capacity plan addresses DCLA's ability to assess and report, while the shared agenda coordinates many actors and requires standing spaces for collaboration and accountability.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks Delfin to explain capacity plan versus shared agenda

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So for Mauricio, you said Create NYC was asked to be both an agency plan and sector-wide agenda.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference and why the city needs both?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Sure, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The capacity building plan for DCLA is addressing specifically how DCLA, what the conditions are for DCLA to operate and deliver on all the objectives that we have been talking this morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So it has to do with really digging into what are those things that the department or the agency requires to be able to report, to be able to assess.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Assessment is big, as we've seen, data collection and data sharing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: But aside from publishing a large data set like the one that was shared or communicated today, which is amazing, this is something that needs to happen daily, and it really needs a coordinated effort, as you also have pointed out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: That's one part of the capacity building that we haven't only talked about it here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: It's been talked to many, many times through different hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: What are those things that DCLA requires to do the job today, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: That is one discrete kind of investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: The shared agenda piece has to do with what the ecosystem looks like right now in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: There's more networks working together, more coalitions, and we are in the capacity to coordinate better intentions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: That requires the kind of infrastructure that the council and the city could convene, could actually make happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So we think that before a plan, we should create the conditions for that plan to actually be held by many and be able to be distributed in a way that we can all participate in uplifting and continuing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: its objectives and holding ourselves accountable for the assessment and the outputs that plan could deliver.

chapters.summary: Delfin says Council's neighborhood-level mandates allow more nuanced resourcing of communities, and a shared agenda would break silos by coordinating executive and legislative roles; Casals adds that oversight can be built into the plan.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks how Council and DCLA would share a cultural agenda

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, you mentioned the council's role.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So do you have a sense of what a shared agenda could be between, you know, the council's role and the CLA?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: I think that one of the advantages of thinking about it as a shared agenda is that the mandates of the different institutions and actors in the system allow us to dig deep into very specific dimensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: For example, the councils and the way that council members come from a specific borough or neighborhood allows us to have a conversation at a neighborhood level like the SIEP team has recommended.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: There's a lot more nuance in that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: We would be talking about resourcing neighborhoods and communities rather than just acting through a patronage model, put it like that way, where you fund an artist or an organization, which is also important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: But our conversation and the repertoire for action would expand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So DCLA's mandate and what they're doing with the programs they have, as you said, there's an executive prerogative, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: With the council, it's of a different sort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: We can talk about Sukasa and all these different ways of articulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So it allows us to represent that complexity and operationalize our actions through coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: A lot of the criticisms that come up is how we work in silos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: This is a way of attending that problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And if you may, the same way that you build evaluation in any plan, you could build oversight in that plan, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Just all of us think together what our site would look like so nobody's surprised when questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: And I'll add one more thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: It's interesting because also in the last years, the capacity of organizations to produce research has increased in a way filling the gaps of the research that doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: So there's a lot of high specialization in each organization that brought together to the table to attend shared problems would be very beneficial.

chapters.summary: Casals says the public artist in residence program is a good first step but remains discrete projects; as policy it would embed artists across agencies, bring new funding, and treat culture as cross-sector infrastructure.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks Casals how artist residencies could become citywide policy

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Gonzalo, you mentioned the public artist in residence as a residency.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What would it look like as a citywide policy?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful to understand, like, how can we make this a policy versus just sort of a residency?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, it's a great program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: I think it should be doing more of that and invest much more on artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: But again, right, that was the first step that the de Blasio administration took, you know, 12 years ago into embedding culture in every aspect of city life, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: But it's just one artist doing a project, discrete project here and there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We need to think about cross-sector immediately for many reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: One is we want to be self-serving, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: But that's the way we're going to be able to be able to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: to bring new funds to the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Two is we have this incredible, as Sayyaf said, this incredible infrastructure of cultural organizations that could be doing so much more, right, if we all plan, you know, in a way that with coordination and intention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: I think, you know, in a way what we're trying to do is we're trying to put a square peg through a hole, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The way we distribute resources, resources for cultural organizations in the city of New York is through a patronage model, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: It looks like we're in the 19th century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The Department of Health spends more money on the South Bronx because there are higher asthma rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Why we cannot spend more money in culture knowing that it has all this incredible impact that we just learned from our friends in SIEP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: So make the policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Make it not just a residency of an artist, but let's cultural policy how it can affect other policies across the city.

chapters.summary: Casals says government's convening power carries leadership responsibility, and the sector needs a clear agenda; Delfin adds that any next step must rest on institutional capacity to assess and deliver.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks how Council should use CreateNYC's 10-year mark

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, and final loaded question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As Create NYC reached its 10-year mark in 2027, how should the council use this moment?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if this committee could take one step to move things forward, what should it be?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: You know, there's a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: One is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: I always say that government has a lot of power because of funding, but also has a power of convening, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And that power of convening comes with a responsibility of leadership, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We all feel in the sector that we're a little unfocused because we don't have, you know, that agenda that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: So how the council and the city administration can say, this is what we see, this is what we hear from our constituencies, this is what we're going to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And each of us, from our organizations, our roles, our missions, the resources that we have, we could all be plugging into that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: I'll just add that I think we need to create as well everything that Gonzalo said, but for that to rest on a capacity that can deliver.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mauricio Delfin
utterances.text: We can talk about all these things, but if an institutional capacity is not able to really assess and provide the knowledge that we need to operationalize, that will be a failure in that next step.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And if you allow me 30 seconds more, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The other thing that we're seeing is we have been talking about how arts and culture can serve, you know, the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We also are an object of policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And one of the things that we're seeing is, and I hinted a little bit, is when big development comes to a neighborhood,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: we make sure that we provide fire, safety, library, schools, parks, but we left arts and culture to the market.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Because we're private partners on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We're not planning, you know, for the long term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We're not planning for the long term creation of those cultural assets that SIAP has mentioned are important to a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And when changes come, we're not even thinking about how we wrote them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Kensington is one of the examples of neighborhoods that are being under, you know, rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: You mentioned, you know, in Queens to go Queens, get the money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: If it's not for advocates like you, right, you know, there's nothing codified that looks at, you know, where are the cultural organizations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: What are the cultural assets that need to be anchored there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And how do we attract new ones as we're going through redevelopment?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm wondering if that's a bill, because I remember the council passed a law that requires racial impact statements on rezonings.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I'm thinking about, you know, we have environmental impact.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I mean, to your point, there are checklists of things that we have to do when we do neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I don't think arts and culture is institutionalized in the same way.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So maybe that is an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: The only way we have a, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: I'm excited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: We had a policy recommendation that really looks at how we start looking at arts and culture assets as community amenities in the environmental impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: And the only way that arts and culture enter now through that process is if, you know, there's a big brick and mortar landmark building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Casals
utterances.text: So that says a lot about.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: A part of why I entered for ours is because we had J-Cal, J-PAC and King Manor.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In the study map.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we sort of had to talk about it because we had these sort of three cultural brick and mortar locations that were within the study map.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So that's definitely a good point.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Every time you come, I'm like, I need to have a separate meeting.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I'm going to try to make it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: that happened so I can like sit down and talk to you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Lucy Sexton of New Yorkers for Culture and Arts calls for revisiting the Disability Forward Fund, creating a permanent cultural advisory group, funding arts education, supporting immigrant and queer artists, and addressing healthcare and affordable workspace.
chapters.title: Lucy Sexton testifies remotely on disability access, arts education, and affordability

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, Lucy is online in London and she can't stay long.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we're gonna call her after this panel.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: This is the entire note and this is what it said.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi, Lucy, joining us from London.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You love us so much that you are zooming in from Big Ben.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: I couldn't miss it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: I have to come over here for work, but I'm coming back on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Thank you very much for hearing my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: I really, really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Chair Williams, Council Members Maloney, Lewis Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: My name is Lucy Sexton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: She, her, I lead New Yorkers for Culture and Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Create NYC identified many problems and proposed solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: It also inspired the People's Cultural Plan, which identified and proposed solutions to further challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: I thank the many people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Who worked on both those plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Create NYC included disability access, inclusion, and equity throughout the plan, articulating the importance of including cultural workers with disabilities in decision-making capacities like grant panels and capital project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: It also created the Disability Forward Fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Both of these ideas should be revisited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: The data on what they achieved and didn't achieve should be released, and we should most importantly get disabled artists and activists back at the table for real change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: One current initiative the city could support right now is the cultural access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: NYC project to research and build an accessibility hub, which would provide low-cost equipment and services allowing cultural organizations of every size to increase accessibility for artists and audiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Create NYC also proposed a Citizens Council and created a Cultural Affairs Advisory Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Neither is active today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: We propose that the City Council pass legislation to make a cultural advisory group a permanent feature, one that would meet with DCLA on a biannual basis to discuss concerns and to see what can be done to address them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Create NYC called for quality arts education for every student, yet we still do not have a dedicated art teacher in every New York City public school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Create NYC emphasized equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Here are some concrete actions to take toward that goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: In serving embattled immigrant artists, the city can help those communities be aware of and receive info on the council's cultural immigrant initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Trusted messengers like the Asian American Arts Alliance should be funded to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: In serving Black and other organizations of color, which are at great risk of cultural erasure due to federal attacks, the Council should increase funding to the Coalition of Theaters of Color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Finally, queer art is mentioned but not meaningfully addressed in the plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: The Council's LGBTQIA plus caucus has advanced a trans artist microgrant program, and they call for a $5 million fund for queer art.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: In this time of attack on queer and trans art, the city should stand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: step in to proudly support these artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: The People's Cultural Plan went further and addressed affordability and support for artists and culture workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: These should be included.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Healthcare for arts workers is in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Many were recently dumped from the Essential Plan due to federal cuts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: City Council should advance the proposal from Freelancers Union to create a pilot program providing portable health benefits for teaching artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: To address, in terms of affordable workspace for artists, philanthropic support has been withdrawn for a longstanding subsidy program that made subsidies so you get affordable rehearsal space for dance and theater artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: That has dried up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: The city should step in with simple subsidies distributed through the art service organizations that have already been doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: To address affordable housing, the city can and should, at no cost, pass legislation guaranteeing that the city's human rights law not be used to ban artist preference housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: This would provide a pathway for nonprofit housing projects to increase the number of affordable apartments for the city's cultural workforce, many of whom are living at or near the poverty line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: To increase the amount of affordable cultural space for organizations, the city should look at the New York State Art Space Act, which proposed tax breaks for developers who offer cultural nonprofits below market rates on 20-year leases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Finally, I want to lift up this idea of culture as civic infrastructure, which you've just been saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: speaking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: As the city looks at its new housing initiatives, it should do an environmental scan, not only of the neighborhood schools and hospitals, but of its cultural spaces and arts organizations that will serve the new residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: As you heard from Mark and Susan, the researchers, data shows that robust cultural assets make for happier, healthier,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: better educated, and more connected communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: So let's build them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Lucy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You answered all the questions we had.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But if you could submit your testimony, though, because you have some really substantive solutions here.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if you could also share, I don't think I've ever seen the People's Culture Plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So if you could send that to me, too, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Get some rest.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We're ahead, right?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They're ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: It's nighttime here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, so get some rest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucy Sexton
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Judith Ensel, executive director of Bronx Arts Ensemble, urges the next CreateNYC to be a true three-to-five-year strategic plan with budget information and for arts and culture funding to reach 1% of the NYC budget.
chapters.title: Judith Ensel calls for a three-to-five-year strategic plan and 1% arts funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: Natasha Williams and any other esteemed city council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: My name is Judith Nitzel, and as the Executive Director of the Bronx Arts Ensemble, I am advocating for the next iteration of Create NYC

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: to be developed as a true three- to five-year strategic plan, including budgetary information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: For years, I have longed for a citywide strategic plan for arts and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: The next Create NYC should be a strategic plan to help all arts institutions, particularly small and mid-sized

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: organizations, move into more sustainable and elevated service of arts and culture programs to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: I would also advocate that this new plan

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: present the real need for arts and culture funding to finally reach 1% in the New York City budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: I believe that setting aside at least this amount of funding in the New York City budget is the only way to successfully execute a new plan for arts and culture in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: Today we have heard testimony from experts citing that cultural

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: assets in communities literally help improve the physical lives of citizens in lower and moderate income neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: My community Bronx-based organization needs to have a supportive citywide plan in place to help us supply the underserved communities of the Bronx to live better and shine brighter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: New York City is a special place that needs support from a very thoughtful strategic plan for arts and culture in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: The next iteration of Create NYC must strive to be a strategic plan that is executed with intention in order to keep pace with the ever-evolving landscape of arts and culture in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judith Ensel
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Lisa Gold of Asian American Arts Alliance says there are no AAPI-led CIGs, only 5% of CDF grantees are AAPI-led despite 18% of the population, and Manhattan's Chinatown lacks a black box theater or public performance space.
chapters.title: Lisa Gold testifies on AAPI underfunding and lack of cultural space

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: Okay, good afternoon, Chair Williams, members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: My name is Lisa Gold, and I'm the Executive Director of the Asian American Arts Alliance, or A4 for short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: For more than 40 years, A4 has worked to ensure greater representation, equity, and opportunities for Asian American and Pacific Islanders, artists, and cultural organizations across all the disciplines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: And I'm really appreciative of you for holding this hearing today on Create NYC because I really do believe that the intentions of the plan were well-meaning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: But as we've all heard, the execution fell way short of expectations and what is truly needed to ensure equity and inclusion in the city's cultural sector, which was obviously the first issue that the plan sought to address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: So we work with a community of artists and arts organizations who receive far less than their equitable share of funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: There are no AAPI-led or serving CIGs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: And from the CDF data last year, which I had to pull myself, it shows that only 5% of organizations who received those CDF grants were AAPI-led and serving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: We are 18% of the city population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: And of those who did receive grants, the average grant amount was 28% less than the average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: So I think that DCA should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: and releasing this data so that we can track and ensure accountability to ensure that underserved communities, which you brought up again, thank you, are actually getting their fair share and getting the resources that they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: And I also want to point out that I think that the local arts...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: Council should also be held to the same standard so we can assure that individual artists are being treated equitably in the distribution of city-funded grants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: So the economic impact of the arts and all of the other health measures

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: is undeniable as we've heard earlier, and yet not all of our communities are benefiting from the city's economic and other development strategies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: For example, Manhattan's Chinatown does not have a single black box theater or public performance space or rehearsal space, and yet the city has managed to find nearly $4 billion to invest in the jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: So I ask that the commission truly engage with communities, especially the members of the AAPI community, 1.5 million of us, to truly ensure equitable and inclusive arts and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lisa Gold
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kimberly Olsen of NYC Arts and Education Roundtable says Strategy 5 lacks a shared definition of high-quality arts education, 69% of eighth graders fail state arts requirements, and urges closing the certified arts teacher gap and modernizing CASA funding.
chapters.title: Kimberly Olsen calls for arts education baseline, teacher pipeline, and data transparency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Williams and members of the City Council staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: My name is Kimberly Olson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: I'm here testifying on behalf of the New York City Arts and Education Roundtable regarding Strategy 5 and Create NYC provide a high quality arts education for all New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: While Create NYC offers a strong framework, it's quite troubling to me to see that the last publicly recorded actions for Strategy 5 date back to 2022.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: To your point earlier, Deputy Speaker, across the CREAT NYC materials, there lacks actually a shared baseline definition of what we actually mean when we say high-quality sequential arts education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: While there are buzzwords and terms thrown around like culturally responsive pedagogy, certified arts teachers, without actually a cleared shared definition, it's near impossible for us to measure what real progress has taken place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: What we do know is that arts education relies on a strong partnership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Last year, last school year alone, over 900 cultural organizations partnered with New York City Public Schools, serving 84% of schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Partnership here is key, but as I think you can see, that partnership needs work between DCLA and New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: To build on this momentum, we urge the city to focus on four critical actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: First, close the certified arts teacher gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Currently, 69% of middle school or eighth grade students are failing to meet arts requirements set by the state, largely because their schools lack a certified arts teacher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Applying the lessons learned from the 2020

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: 2019 Staten Island pilot that helped bring more certified arts teachers into our system, leveraging the PE Works model, and also using the baseline funding for arts education can help our city close the gap and ensure that students receive a sequential arts instruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Second, help reconnect schools with local arts partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Since Create NYC launched, the city actually discontinued both the Arts and Cultural Education Services Guide and the annual Arts Services Fair, leaving schools without a clear roadmap to cultural partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: We applaud you, Deputy Speaker, for hosting an upcoming CASA fair and urge the city to expand this model to at least one fair per district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: We are happy to help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: To help bridge this gap as well, the Roundtable is launching a platform called Creative Compass in late 26, early 27.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: That's going to be a searchable arts partner database.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: However, we need clear collaboration with New York City Public Schools, with DOE, and with the council to make it a success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Third, we ask that you modernize CASA funding and contracting timelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: The CASA programming is a model initiative, but grant amounts remain static since its inception, while the cost of living and the cost of delivering programs have skyrocketed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: With award letters being released as late as March, it leaves little time for program delivery that's only a fraction of the school year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Moving to quarterly award letters and increasing grant sizes not only helps put teaching artists to work, but also helps deliver free programming to families starting earlier in the school year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: And last but not least, just improving data transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: In 2025, the independent budget...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: reported that 72% of schools have at least one CDF-funded program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Requiring grantees who are working in schools to include school DBN in their final reports will yield important data to help identify potential arts deserts and guide equitable funding allocations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: DJ McDonald describes the Dance Parade and the Cultural Accessibility NYC project, which is researching disability justice and cultural access, and calls for disability equity to be a first consideration in cultural planning.
chapters.title: DJ McDonald testifies on Cultural Accessibility NYC and disability justice

utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Staff members, and all my friends, colleagues, and fellow art advocates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: research and planning phase and hoping to publish its findings and recommendations for furthering disability justice and cultural access for artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Culture workers and audiences across New York City's cultural landscape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: At least three of my colleagues and advisors working on this initiative also plan to testify in the course of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald

utterances.text: and philanthropic partners, if we can address the promises that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: that fell through the original plan and action plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: We can together try to reach their goals and recommendations to make disability justice and equity among the first and not the last considerations in approaching the possibilities inherited in the vast wealth

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: of our city's cultural landscape and heritage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: As a dancer aging as fast as nature makes necessary, this is as much an affordable, this is as this as much affordable space

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: will make this a more livable, colorful, and vibrant city we love for ourselves as well as many of our fellow New Yorkers as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Cindy VandenBosch, lead consultant for Cultural Accessibility NYC, describes surveys and focus groups on accessibility infrastructure, asks for DCLA data, and questions how Disability Forward Fund money was distributed.
chapters.title: Cindy VandenBosch testifies on cultural accessibility research and Disability Forward Fund

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams, as well as other members of the City Council staff and those that are here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: My name is Cindy Vandenbosch, and I am the president of Turnstile Tours and Studio.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: I have over 20 years of experience working to advance accessibility in the cultural and tourism fields in New York City, and I've also worked for disability service providers through the years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: I'm delivering my testimony today from the perspective of a non-disabled cultural accessibility practitioner, researcher, and planner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: I'm currently the lead consultant on this research and planning project for Cultural Accessibility NYC, and we are taking an evidence-based and collaborative

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: approach and are seeking to take collective action to advance the city's arts and culture sector towards experiential equity for and with disabled workers, artists, and audiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: I'm currently working alongside a team of researchers and steering committee of artists, cultural access workers, and advocates, most of whom have lived experience with disability, to gather quantitative and qualitative data

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: on the state of the city's cultural accessibility infrastructure to inform strategies to address systemic barriers and aggregate resources to better support organizations'accessibility capacity building efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: This research seeks to build on past efforts, including the cultural plan and all the hard work that many, many disability advocates and cultural accessibility experts invested in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We also seek to, we're conducting a landscape analysis literature review and a survey, which is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: live through the end of the week, targeting cultural workers about organizational structures and needs, as well as focus groups with deaf and disabled artists, disability service providers, and cultural workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We welcome the city to engage with this project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We need the city to engage with this project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: As we've been doing this research, you know, we've thought to ourselves, what would it mean if we could actually gain access to some of the data that the Department of Cultural Affairs actually has in its applications?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: I will also say that since my time is short, a priority from our perspective is this question around nothing about us without us, the disability rights mantra.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: You know, Simi Linton and Kevin Gottkin from the Disability Arts NYC Task Force who mobilized so many people

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: to work on the cultural plan, they're not here today and they need to be at the table, as do other leaders in disability arts and cultural accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: How can we integrate accessibility into the way that organizations carry out their work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: And what's going on with the Disability Forward Fund that was designed to increase equity and inclusion of artists, cultural workers, and audiences with disabilities?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We're asked today to comment on where we go from here, but we don't even know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We know that there were some funds distributed, but how were they distributed across the objective?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: There were multiple different objectives for that fund, and there's no sort of public sense of how those funds have been used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: And last but not least, I think this is for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We do want to, I'm excited to hear that there will be more data that's available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: But for example, on the CDF application, it asks thousands of organizations, what are your specific strategies and policies to make programs accessible to people with disabilities?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Outline your practices that go beyond ADA compliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Imagine what we could learn if we all took a step back and there was actually analysis that was done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Why is it that we don't have researchers in-house at the Department of Cultural Affairs as the County of LA has?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: They actually are able to do that analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Is it a capacity?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: building issue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: You know, is there a way that there can be partnerships that are formed with organizations that are in and of these communities that can support analysis so that we know what has been accomplished and we're not starting from scratch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: We need to build on the hard work that's been done on this cultural plan and understand what has been accomplished and where do we go from here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cindy VandenBosch
utterances.text: Thank you.
