chapters.summary: Chris Gorman of the Museum of the City of New York, speaking for CIG chair Stephanie Hill Wilchfort, describes CIG's 39 institutions, 4 million free visits, 15,700 employees, and educational partnerships, and offers CIG as a partner for future plans.
chapters.title: Chris Gorman testifies for Cultural Institutions Group on CreateNYC partnership

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Williams and members of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Intergroup Relations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: My name is Chris Gorman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: I'm Vice President of Public Affairs at the Museum of the City of New York, and I am honored to speak on behalf of Stephanie Hill Wilchfort, the museum's Rone Menschel Director and Chair of the Cultural Institutions Group, who could not be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: I'm here to provide testimony on behalf of the CIG, a coalition of 39 cultural organizations located in all five boroughs, including zoos, gardens, museums, and performing arts organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Our institutions have been partners in Create NYC since it launched in 2017.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Nine years later, I want to share some of the ways our institutions execute on the goals of Create NYC and to offer the CIG as a partner of the city in developing future cultural plans for a new era.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: On a personal note, my daughter was born in October of 2017, and I'm grateful she arrived in a city where culture and museums are supported and championed and continue to be, thanks to you and your committee members, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: The goal of Create NYC was to build a more inclusive, equitable, and resilient cultural ecosystem and to examine how cultural

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: equity can be advanced through government policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: As public institutions, the CIGs have worked under the longstanding mission to ensure culture is affordable and accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Our institutions welcome over 4 million free visits each year and serve as safe public spaces for people of all ages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Each of our institutions expands its reach through partnerships,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: with city agencies and community-based organizations to provide a host of services that complement our core missions, such as implementing the IDNYC program and serving as vaccination sites, voting sites, and cooling centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Our institutions have 15,700 full and part-time employees, including 5,800 union staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: CIGs also employ approximately 6,000 per DM staff members, including teaching artists, musicians, explainers, educators, and other professionals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: We train the city's cultural workforce, and we draw cultural workers and creative industries to New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: The CIG is essential to the city's economic prosperity and should continue to be integrated into the city's economic development strategy in both workforce development and attracting talent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: The CIG's educational resources for New York City students make New York a leader in museum education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: For example, in the last year at the Museum of the City of New York, we welcomed over 15,000 students on over 700 field trips.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Each field trip is offered in English and Spanish or with bilingual support, and all of our exhibitions offer feature labels in English and Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Public and charter schools in East Harlem visit for free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Much like our peers across the CIG, our institutions also serve as essential partners for our public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Public support is critical in order for our institutions to execute their missions and to deliver high-quality educational experiences for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: We are deeply grateful for the City Council and the Mumdani administration's historic commitment to culture in fiscal year 27.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify as allies in helping the city execute key initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: We look forward to strengthening our partnership and exploring new areas of collaboration to ensure that cultural workers can afford to live here, every child gets arts education, and every New Yorker is welcomed into our institutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Gorman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Martha Nabors of Snug Harbor Cultural Center says CreateNYC inspired diversity and accessibility changes, but cultural workers earn 23% less than national average, artists are leaving NYC, and the city must act to stem the creative brain drain.
chapters.title: Martha Nabors testifies on Snug Harbor and cultural workforce challenges

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Williams and council staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the shout out to Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: We do appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: I am Martha Nabors, Executive Vice President of Snug Harbor Cultural Center and Botanical Garden, a culture park and member of the Cultural Institutions Group located in Council District 49 on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: I'm here today on behalf of Jessica Vador, President and CEO and Vice Chair for Staten Island of the Cultural Institutions Group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Create NYC was instrumental in building a more inclusive and equitable cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Snug Harbor is encouraged to see Council and the Department of Cultural Affairs revisiting the plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: While progress has been made towards its objectives, there is still much work to do to ensure that all New Yorkers can have access to culture and that artists and cultural workers can build sustainable lives in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Inspired by the original plan, Snug Harbor has revamped recruitment, hiring, and promotion, building a more diverse staff and board of directors, and screens all of our programs for inclusion and accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: We address affordability through artist residencies and free and deeply discounted rental fees for artists, cultural organizations, and community groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Since the 2019 action plan was released, visitorship has increased 30%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: This work is ongoing as our goal is a more culturally connected and thriving Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: The creative sector in New York City is facing major challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Cultural workers earn 23% less than the national average when adjusted for the high cost of living in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Rising insurance costs in a gig economy make health care unattainable for many.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Housing and workspace is unaffordable for most of our artists and young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: New York City's resident artist population is declining.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Artists and young people are leaving our city for better quality of life elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: New York's creative ecosystem is inseparable from our civic identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Arts and culture generates over $110 billion annually and employs over 325,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Our sector is a key driver for tourism, which generates an additional $74 billion in economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: New York City does not work without a vibrant cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: To stem the creative brain drain and ensure a vibrant cultural sector, the city must take action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Create NYC has largely sat on a shelf over the last six or seven years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: A revitalized plan, well executed, would lead to a more sustainable, diverse, inclusive, and equitable cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: As originally envisioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Snug Harbor applauds City Council, the administration, and the Department of Cultural Affairs for your collective commitment to a health

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: and vibrant cultural sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: We are eager to partner with you to ensure that Staten Island plays a role in making our city the center of creativity and innovation that we all know it should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Nabors
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Malik Jones, chief people officer at Lincoln Center, describes free and choose-what-you-pay performances reaching nearly 3 million people, a new performance park opening in 2028, and calls for the next plan to operationalize culture as essential infrastructure.
chapters.title: Malik Jones testifies on Lincoln Center access and culture as essential infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: My name is Malik Jones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: I'm the Chief People Officer at Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We believe culture is critical to democracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: This means it must be accessible, affordable, and reflective of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Create NYC solidified the city's commitment to this issue, shaped a clear set of policy goals, and historic investments in culture are steps in continuing this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: At Lincoln Center, this has meant a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: One, affordable access to art.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Since 2022, Lincoln Center presents free and choose what you pay model has helped bring nearly 3 million people to our campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: This approach welcomes more people and reflects our commitment to centering the arts in everyday life, ensuring extraordinary artistic experiences remain within reach for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Next, art spaces as civic spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: In 2028, we'll be excited to open the re-envisioned Amsterdam Avenue from the library to Damaraj Park to a new performance park designed with over 7,200 insights from community members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: also strengthened our relationships in the neighborhood, hosting community board meetings, collaborating with nearby NYCHA neighbors, and engaging surrounding schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: And centered inclusive practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Our work benefits from the broad range of perspectives and experiences that our management team and our employees bring to this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We're also investing in the next generation through expanded recruitment, including participating in New York City at Work and summer youth employment through the Access Ambassadors Program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: As the city plans for the next iteration, we need the cultural plan to evolve into New York City's operationalization of culture as essential infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We must, one, leverage every tool and create new mechanisms so New Yorkers can afford to live, create, and present in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We must connect every New Yorker to culture in a way that is attainable and accessible and deploy across agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Effort that incorporates culture in all aspects to build healthier, more connected, and resilient communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We offer more details in our written submission, but in closing, without bold solutions, we risk losing our city's identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: Together, we believe we can be part of the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Malik Jones
utterances.text: We thank you again for your time.

chapters.summary: Rosalind Barbour of the Public Theater says CreateNYC helped focus free mobile unit performances in low-income communities like Brownsville and St. Mary's Park, and that the required DEI plan helped the theater center anti-racism.
chapters.title: Rosalind Barbour testifies on Public Theater's use of CreateNYC research

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Williams, Council Members and Staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: I'm Rosalind Barber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: I'm the Administrative Chief of Staff at the Public Theater.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Thank you for this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Every year, the public serves over 100,000 New Yorkers with free programming, including Shakespeare in the Park, our mobile unit performances in the five boroughs, and free classes for seniors, youth, immigrants, and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Create NYC has helped us do that work with greater focus because a clear plan makes us a more effective partner with the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Here are a few examples of what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: In the Create NYC plan, it called for supporting the cultural life of low-income communities and derived research from the CAP study to help identify those communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: We used that same research, having read the cultural plan, to help us identify where we would take our mobile unit performances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: So it really helped galvanize that idea, picking up from the research that already existed to allow us to focus our efforts in a way that made sense in the context of the cultural plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: So with that, we've renewed our focus in going to places like Brownsville Rec, St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Mary's Park, Roy Wilkins Park, Faber Fieldhouse, and many other locations across the city, all of the performances being free with no RSVP required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: It's also why we partner with libraries and in all five boroughs to distribute our free Shakespeare in the Park tickets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Second, the Create NYC plan required a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: board adopted EDI or DEI plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: And while the public was already in the process of creating that and had a committee, this again was a really galvanizing force that helped us when we were having conversations with our board explain the necessity to have these plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: And since then, we've revised our plan to center anti-racism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: We still have work to do, but having this plan has made us better, and it's also sort of ensured that we're having this conversation with our board and with our staff in a really thoughtful way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: What makes this work is clarity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: When the city states its expectations clearly, we know what we're accountable for, and we can hold the city accountable as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: That shared accountability creates dialogue and shared purpose, and it improves our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: So we hope that there will be a revitalized and intentional, I feel like that was a word that previous folks used, commitment to this plan, where we can all join together and be a force amplifier in this important work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Barbour
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Daniel Arnow of the Entertainment Community Fund and Housing Development Corporation says the resident artist population is declining, and calls for city-led developments to include cultural facilities, affordable artist housing, and an artist preference in affordable housing.
chapters.title: Daniel Arnow testifies on artist housing and affordable workspace

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: My name's Daniel Arno.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: I'm here on behalf of the Entertainment Community Fund and our Housing Development Corporation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: We are a human service organization that provides support, including affordable housing, to everyone in the performing arts and entertainment community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: I'm here with Esther and Randy to discuss Create NYC's Objective 4, which is focused on the affordability crisis, real estate, and our cultural community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Arts and culture are New York City's greatest asset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Arts workers are the engine of our creative community and strengthen communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Yet, New York City's resident artist population is declining for the first time in decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: This situation is driven by the affordability crisis, the high cost of real estate, and rising cost of living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Arts and culture are a public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: It requires strong infrastructure and intentional city planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: A critical question for us is how do we preserve and create long-term affordable artist workspace and artist housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: To start, city-led developments can explicitly include cultural facilities and affordable housing for artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: These priorities should be built into the initial planning, RFP process, and include DCLA as a partner from the outset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: For affordable artist workspace within mixed-use affordable affordable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: housing developments, the city should create a streamlined and dedicated pathway that enables arts organizations to partner with developers, access capital funding for the fit out of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: This would help deliver cultural spaces more quickly while reducing risk, cost, and uncertainty for stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: On the housing front, we need more affordable housing for all New Yorkers, and we also need dedicated programs that are designed to address the unique needs of our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: New York needs a little bit of artist housing everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: One mechanism to achieve this is an artist's preference in affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: And we do support legislation introduced that would allow the city to establish an artist's preference without violating the human rights law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Arnow
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Randi Berry of Indie Space urges the city to integrate cultural assets into planning, create pathways to permanent affordable cultural space through land trusts and acquisition funds, incentivize cultural space in new development, and streamline capital processes.
chapters.title: Randi Berry testifies on permanent affordable cultural space and land trusts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: My name is Randy Berry, and I'm the Executive Director of Indie Space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: We are a community organizer and a grassroots service organization for low-income artists, cultural workers, and small-budget organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: We provide them with funding, professional development, and real estate expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: We believe culture should be treated as a public good and essential social infrastructure, not an amenity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Cultural spaces help create connected, healthy communities, yet the people and organizations that sustain our cultural life are increasingly being priced out of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: We urge the city to enhance CreateMIC by, first,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: You've heard this before today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Integrating cultural assets into city planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: This is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Cultural space should be considered essential infrastructure alongside housing, schools, and parks, and incorporated into neighborhood planning from the beginning, not something that we try to accommodate after development decisions have already been made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Second, create pathways to permanent affordable cultural space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Explore creative land trusts, the use of city-owned properties, and a dedicated acquisition fund that allows arts organizations to act quickly enough to actually compete in the real estate market.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Third, incentivize cultural space and new development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Create density bonuses for developers that are providing free or deeply affordable space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: and refine community facility definitions so that small cultural organizations can compete for these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Including cultural space in a building is only meaningful if artists can actually afford to use it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Fourth, streamline the process for creating cultural space in affordable housing developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: The process of financing and building out cultural space can be complicated and very slow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Through HPD and other relevant agencies, simplifying the capital process and allowing organizations and developers to work and fundraise in tandem for cultural space build-outs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: At IndieSpace, we work every day to fill the gaps that existing systems leave behind, but artists cannot be expected to solve a systemic affordability crisis through creativity and resilience alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: We need public policies that make cultural space possible, affordable, and permanent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: New York's cultural life is one of its greatest public assets, and the city's cultural plan must help ensure that the people who create that culture actually have a future here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Berry
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Esther Robinson of ArtBuilt describes 50,000 square feet of affordable workspace at Brooklyn Army Terminal, calls for cultural production to be an economic priority, and urges 20-year leases for publicly owned cultural production space.
chapters.title: Esther Robinson testifies on cultural production space and long-term leases

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Williams and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: I'm Esther Robinson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of Art Built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: At the Brooklyn Army Terminal, we operate about 50,000 square feet of affordable workspace for more than 120 artists and creative businesses created through the city's area initiative in 2016 and 2017, as mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Art Built remains the largest nonprofit, long-term, affordable creative workspace built in New York City in the past 30 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: That's a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: And we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Oh, it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: We want more in Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: I'm with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: There should be more art belts everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: And we've seen what stable production space makes possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: These businesses hire, they train, they export, and they build lives in this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: So I want to focus on something often missing from cultural planning, where culture is made, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Behind our theaters, films, fashion, dance, and visual arts are workplaces, skilled trades, small businesses, and entire networks of production.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: The next Create NYC must make cultural production an economic priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Every borough and every council district needs places where goods and cultural work are made at scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: These are working places, not simply cultural amenities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: The city needs to deliberately plan for, invest in, and build the spaces where this work happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: And we need to build for generations, not development or political cycles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: ArtBuild shows what city-owned space plus nonprofit operation can accomplish, but short leases are undermining financing and long-term investment in a very big way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: The next plan needs to commit to leases of at least 20 years for publicly owned cultural production space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Our written testimony also proposes a permanent cultural production infrastructure fund and measures to track whether production space is actually growing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: We don't even know what our loss rate is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: The opportunity is bigger than any single project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: We can build a citywide network of places where New Yorkers make things, build businesses, and invest in their neighborhoods across generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Let's build a New York where the next generation doesn't just inherit a cultural legacy, but where every New Yorker inherits the means

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: to create the greatest cultural capital in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esther Robinson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Deeksha Gaur, executive director of TDF, says TDF served 1.3 million audience members, partnered on Tickets for Teens giving 2,000 free tickets, and urges the next plan to prioritize affordability and access for audiences.
chapters.title: Deeksha Gaur testifies on TDF's Tickets for Teens and arts access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: My name is Biksha Gore, and I'm the executive director

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Director of TDF.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: I'm proud to be here on behalf of the 1.3 million audience members TDF served last year, including New Yorkers from all 51 council districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: TDF's work is driven by a core belief that when people experience art, they and their communities are better for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Arts participation reduces loneliness and depression, and it increases civic-mindedness, including our propensity to vote, volunteer, and donate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: That's why our programs connect communities to the theater at every level, through the TKTS booth and our membership programs, through our education programs and community partnerships, and through our physical accessibility work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: In August of this year, TDF partnered with city and cultural institutions, including the Department of Cultural Affairs, on Tickets for Teens, giving away 2,000 free theater tickets to New York City's high schoolers, along with a free

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: TDF membership, unlocking deeply discounted access to the arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Over 23,000 students signed up in five days and purchased or unlocked over 5,000 admissions, highlighting our community's appetite for arts and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: As you consider the next steps for Create NYC and the city's cultural agenda, I urge you to continue to prioritize affordable...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Affordability and access to the arts for the arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Many New Yorkers today believe that the arts are not for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: The city has the opportunity in its next plan to dispel that myth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: By making the arts affordable, accessible, and welcoming for all New Yorkers, we are investing in the artists and audiences of our future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: And most importantly, we're building a more connected, more engaged, and healthier community for us all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: As Tickets for Teens taught us, we have the best chance of success when we all bring our strengths to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: TDF stands ready to contribute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: We sit at the center of a robust ecosystem of producers, cultural institutions, 150 neighborhood community organizations, schools, audiences, and government agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deeksha Gaur
utterances.text: Together, we hope to lay the foundation for a joyful, healthy, and thriving future for New York and our cultural community.

utterances.text: We have seen increased CDF support as a small organization, but we have not seen DCLA take deliberate action to support vulnerable LGBTQ communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: When we consider the next phase of the Create NYC plan, we must consider how this plan will protect and empower queer, trans, immigrant, and youth artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: With DCLA's recent announcement of a cultural stability fund, we must recognize the instability of queer artists, of queer arts and culture organizations, currently on the front lines of the Trump administration's attacks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Last year, the administration revoked our $20,000 NEA grant just two weeks before we started rehearsals for our annual Criminal Queerness Festival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Now, we are in federal lawsuit against the NEA, represented by the ACLU, looking to overturn their ban on funding programs that promote gender ideology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: We need DCLA and the Council's help to fight back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: To support New York City's vibrant queer arts and culture, we recommend the following additions to the Create NYC plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Number one, baseline $5 million in funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: for queer arts organizations, as outlined in the City Council's LGBTQIA plus caucus's Pride and Policy Plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Two, fund after school programming for LGBTQ youth outside of school settings as an amendment for CASA or outside of CASA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Three, support the Trans Artist Microgrant Program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Advocates have been fighting for an $800,000 initiative, which would support 1,400 New York City trans artists with $500 microgrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: And lastly, continue prioritizing funding for small arts organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: We are closest to our communities and can provide the most direct support to artists with the least bureaucracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kaneza Schaal, a Thai queer immigrant theater artist, describes how National Queer Theater gave her artistic freedom and community, and urges city arts funding to reach the smallest organizations and most vulnerable artists.
chapters.title: Kaneza Schaal testifies on immigrant queer artists and smallest organizations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Dear Speaker Williams, my name is Kang Mehtia Nuat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: I am a Thai queer immigrant theater artist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Sawadee Ka.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: And I'm an executive director of Thai Theater Foundation, also the member of the Artistic Collective at National Queer Theater.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: My relationship with National Queer Theater began when I directed a play called What You Are to Me as part of the Criminal Queerness Festival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: It was one of my first directing gigs in New York City, and it changed the way I understand my place here as both queer artists and immigrant artists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: I grew up in Thailand where censorship in art is real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: So directing a work that explored queer censorship felt deeply personal to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: As a queer immigrant artist, we often carry those experiences with questioning whether this piece

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: is too political, too queer, too cultural specific, or too simple, or even too difficult for someone to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: But working with National Queer Theater taught me that those stories do not have to remain untold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: And they have a space and the audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: New York City have given me artistic freedom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Just importantly, New York City has given me a friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: So that might sound funny and something to tell the city council, but I mean it seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: For all...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Friendship becomes community, community becomes collaboration, and someone invites you to a project and you introduce them to someone else and then they form a project together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: And that network is often what keeps us growing when this career feels impossible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: But community alone cannot pay the bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Today, I run a nonprofit called High Theater Foundation, when even with public support, creating sustainable opportunity for artists is still difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: So I echo Adam's recommendation, and I would like to add tiny things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Please make sure the city arts funding reach the smallest organization and the most vulnerable artists, especially queer artists who works exist in intersection of immigration, race, culture, and identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Queer art should not have to survive only because individual organizations fight to make a room for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: We are not the risk to fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: We are the part that make the city the cultural capital of the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaneza Schaal
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Lindsey Buller Maliekel of New 42 describes a NYCHA partnership giving 2,000 free tickets that sell out quickly, says loss of health insurance drives teaching artists out, and urges continued support for arts education and portable benefits.
chapters.title: Lindsey Buller Maliekel testifies on NYCHA arts access and portable benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Lindsay Molly Aikle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: I'm the Vice President of Education and Public Engagement at the New 42, and we thank the New York City Council and Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Williams for your continued advocacy of cultural organizations like New 42, because resources like Create New York City Cultural Plan are essential to our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We want to offer support for the future of Create NYC, and more specifically, some key objectives and strategies that we hope will continue to be supported robustly as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Objective one talks about support for culture in historically underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: In 2022, we started a partnership with NYCHA, specifically to invite families living in NYCHA housing to participate and attend live performing arts as a family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: This program has grown quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: This year we'll give away 2,000 free tickets, and through our partnership with TDF, we can help connect those families to more and more performing arts opportunities for free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Our ticket allocations have been selling out in under an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: In fact, the one that I did last week was 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We know that there's a huge appetite and New York City families living in NYCHA are hungry to be invited to participate and attend in live performing arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: And we want the future of Create NYC to help expand this kind of access for New York City families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Also, the affordability crisis of the cultural community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: You've talked about it a lot, but to bottom line it, we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: The main reason our teaching artists are having to leave the field is because of the loss of health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: So that portable benefits, we are part of the working group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We are trying to make that work happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We are happy to collaborate as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: But we invest a lot of our direct salary support to our artists who we're working with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: And that's the thing that is kicking them out of making art and staying in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We'd also like to make sure that providing high-quality arts education for all New York City public school students stays at the forefront.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: Kim Olson talked about it really wonderfully, and so I'm just sort of bringing up a lot of what she said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: But one of the things that we want to talk about is that the research that we've been doing about what happens for kids who are getting to attend live performing arts is really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: And if we take kids out of our idea about what it means to provide cultural access for New York City, we're really losing a huge amount of impact for this city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: So we just want to thank you for reinvesting in this and reengaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lindsey Buller Maliekel
utterances.text: We are very, very appreciative.

chapters.summary: Sherelle Dixon of Pan African Solutions Consulting describes nonprofit capacity constraints, local and global cultural disconnect, and cultural preservation gaps, and asks for a dedicated funding stream for for-profit MWBE firms to partner with CBOs.
chapters.title: Sherelle Dixon testifies on MWBE engagement and cultural preservation gaps

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yeah, you can start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sora, Deputy Speaker, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Williams, my current and former council members, Osei and Hudson, in their absence, fellow members of the Committee of Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Thank you so much for having us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: My name is Chevelle Dixon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: I'm the founder and managing director of Pan African Solutions Consulting, and I bring you greetings from the great Allen Nation of Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: In our 13-year existence, we are New York City MWBE and New York State MWBE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: We also are a New York City DOE vendor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: We specialize in strategic planning and government technical assistance, nonprofit board advisory through program implementation and third-party evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Having worked in 60 countries and 16 within Africa, we amplify economic sovereignty, collaborative opportunities, and cultural engagement across the Black diaspora locally and globally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: In our work, we have observed two critical, well, three critical interconnected gaps across our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: One, or firstly, nonprofit capacity constraints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Grassroots CBOs are on the ground, but they're stretched thin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: They are operating in silos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: They are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: constantly juggling direct services while struggling with compliance for board governance and strategic external relations and coordination constraints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Secondly, local and global cultural disconnect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Neighborhoods are losing their local cultural essence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: From vanishing still pan yards in Brooklyn to underutilized youth library spaces, our youth need workforce exposure and our aging population need engagement that bridges generational understanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Furthermore, there's an opportunity to bridge local cultural with global assets, such as the United Nations and international mission offices calling our very city home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Thirdly, cultural preservation and recognition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: There is an unaddressed gap in mapping and honoring our local cultural giants through a coordinated and transparent way of preserving our neighborhood histories through formal street cone namings and arts and cultural assets such as murals and monuments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: This also provides an opportunity to engage in 400,000, like they just said, NITRA residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: 500,000 NITRA residents where, sorry, I lost my place, are residents to not only be culturally consumers, we're always talking about them being cultural consumers, let's not forget, we are also cultural creators and contributors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: As we all know, hip-hop was founded in 1973 in NITRA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: We've reviewed, us here in Pan-African,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: We reviewed the Create NYC plan and identified structural policy gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: DCLA funding is constrained strictly to nonprofits and individual artists for grants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: It lacks a mechanism for a mission-driven, for-profit MWBE engagement, firms to participate, build capacity, and deliver specialized technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: Our call to action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: As you reimagine Create NYC, we urge this committee to establish a dedicated funding stream,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: modeling successful frameworks such as Citizens NYC, for example, neighborhood business grants, to enable for-profit MWBE engagement firms to partner directly with CBOs and city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: My follow-up request and in conclusion, Pan-African Solutions Consulting welcomes the opportunity to follow up with committee members

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: to share our framework for nonprofit board governance, institutional strengthening, youth and aging civic engagement, NYCHA, resident inclusion, and cultural sustainability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherelle Dixon
utterances.text: I thank you for your time and your leadership.

chapters.summary: Eva Mayhabal Davis of Latinx Arts Consortium says language access funding is unclear, displacement threatens Latinx cultural practices, and urges community ownership of cultural spaces and co-designed portable health benefits for artists.
chapters.title: Eva Mayhabal Davis testifies on language access, affordable space, and portable benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair, Deputy Speaker, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Nantasha Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Good to see you again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: To the City Council and all the support that you do for arts and culture across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: My name is Eva Mayabal-Davis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: I'm here as a project manager for the Latinx Arts Consortium, LXNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: We represent 55-plus Latino-serving cultural organizations across New York City, ranging from artist collectives to a couple of CIGs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Our mission is to foster knowledge sharing and exchange, as well as collective action towards systemic change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Several of our members were part of the multilingual, multiracial coalition of artists, cultural workers, and community organizers that published the People's Cultural Plan in May 2017, the initial response to create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Nearly a decade later, New York City has made progress in several areas identified by that plan,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: yet many of its central concerns remain unresolved, particularly for Latinx, Black, immigrant, indigenous, and other historically under-resourced artists and cultural organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Create NYC includes language for equity throughout the plan, and in order to more effectively comment on that progress that has been made, and as many of my colleagues have also pointed out, we need to know

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: more about the extent of those results since their inception.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: So I really thank you for pushing on making sure that we better understand that data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: In response, I want to uplift three points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: One is language access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Language access and funding was made available and proposed by Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: However, its disbursement and funding is not clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: We cannot, we must support establishing partnerships with service communities with language needs that include translation services, live interpretation, captioning,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: all of the ways in which language works so that we can have English to another language and other mother languages into a multilingual dimension.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: This is especially important as mono speakers are currently being discriminated against through the federal administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: And we know that language is culture and deserves the nuance of human translators who are cultural workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: A second point, affordable cultural spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: It's been addressed by many of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: What has been the impact of the subsidized rehearsal space to this point, which is now coming to an end?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: The People's Cultural Plan identified displacement as one of the greatest threats to cultural life in New York City, arguing that artists cannot thrive when the communities that's a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Staying their work are priced out of neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: For Latinx cultural organizations, especially these pressures, threaten more than physical infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: They jeopardize the community of cultural practices, intergenerational relationships, community-based artistic networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: And we call to community ownership and control of cultural spaces that remain largely unrealized at a systemic level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: And I was very happy to hear more of my colleagues'initiatives for community land trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: In addition, and as we've heard your follow-up on freelance cultural works frequently lacking access to health care, retirement benefits, paid leave, and unpredictable employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: And today, many artists cannot afford the essential plan due to continued defunding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: And so we urge you to continue to consult with us, the experts, on what it means to push forward in co-designing portable benefits for health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Mayhabal Davis
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jerry Mikorenda, author of a book on Elizabeth Jennings Graham, says She Built NYC selected women for statues in 2018 but no progress has been made on four designs, and criticizes DCLA's lack of transparency and delayed FOIL response.
chapters.title: Jerry Mikorenda testifies on stalled She Built NYC statues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: It's on now?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Jerry Mike Arenda, author of America's First Freedom Writer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: In 2018, She Built New York asked residents to nominate and select a woman in each borough for statues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: It seemed like a straightforward project, a layup in basketball terms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Then the pandemic came.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Two administrations changed hands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Three years later, no progress has been made on any of the four new designs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Where have all the statues gone?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: It's been eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: 2027 is around the corner.

utterances.text: In 2019, a memorial to Mother Krabini was put forth in Battery Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: It was dedicated in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: If the city leadership doesn't believe these heroic women deserve statues, it should just say so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Fumbling the ball looks bad on any court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: If the city believes in the program, it should take the shot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: The Knicks finally did, but we're not waiting 53 years for the rock to drop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Deliver the promise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams says the Billie Holiday statue in her district has selected an artist but is delayed, agrees the program has stalled, and promises to follow up with the commissioner and have staff contact Mikorenda.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I love all the basketball analogies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Very New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I thought it was fitting.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, it was very fitting.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I will say the one in my district for Billy Hall.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: has been moving along.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, they selected an artist, but I agree.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I feel like they have been stalled.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And as you heard from my question from Councilman Mamarate, he has issues.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I would say the one in my district, the status they have selected an artist, I don't know what the next step is and the timeline for the next step, but they did select an artist to do the monument.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: For the Billie Holiday one in my district.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So that's my little one update I have for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: That's interesting you should say that because the reason I'm here is, you know, I got involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: You talked about Chris Marte and moving the statue, Jenning's statue from Grand Central to Community Board 1.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: And I was asked three years ago by Community Board 1, because I wrote a book about her, where do you think, where did this actually happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: And so I looked at the old Sanborn fire maps, went down, and I said, well, given, you know, there's all kinds of buildings there now, I said, but it is down here in...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: In Community Board 1.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I also then, because everybody was saying, you know, nobody's getting any information out of cultural affairs, I said, well, what's going on with the program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Is there anything going on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: And nothing happened, so I put in a FOIL request, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: They sent some, and this was a year ago, I put in a FOIL request, and they put in, oh, we need 60 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: The information is so voluminous, we can't get to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Another 60 days, another 60 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I think if I still kept asking, it would have been this November 20th where they said that maybe they would have something.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: So I filed an Article 78 with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I sent it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: You know, certified mail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I never got the card back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: But I finally did get an email from somebody in cultural affairs that said, you know, what can we help you with?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: And I said, well, what's going on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: And they said, nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: There's nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: There's nothing to report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: There's no information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: There's nothing we can send you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: So that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: I said, well, if nothing's happened in eight years, when are they going to start happening?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll follow up with the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: It sounds like I didn't get quite the story that I was told in the email, so I'm a little annoyed by that, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a lack of government transparency because they have been doing things on it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I mean, clearly it is significantly delayed.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: People should be frustrated, but I know they are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, I personally have been actively involved in conversations over the course of the last two years for the one, the Billie Holiday statue in my district.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So they should have provided a more robust update to you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I will follow up with the commissioner on that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And we have your information.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Regina, can we specifically follow up?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Mikorenda
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, no worries.

chapters.summary: Beth Prevor of Hands-On Sign Interpretive Performances says deaf theatergoers still face barriers, the Disability Forward Fund lacks review and accountability, and asks for access reporting from city-funded organizations and real inclusion in decision-making.
chapters.title: Beth Prevor testifies on deaf access and Disability Forward Fund accountability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adam Odsess-Rubin
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you to the committee for this opportunity to testify on Create NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: And I'll be echoing much as what has been already said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: My name is Beth Prevore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I'm a native New Yorker, a disabled person, and co-founder and executive director of Hands-On Sign Interpretive Performances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Which provides interpreting services to a variety of theaters across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I've worked alongside the deaf community for more than 42 years, and I hear their frustrations constantly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I need an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I call the theater.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: They didn't know what I meant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: No one called back, or they just said no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: A quick no gets everyone off the hook, and the deaf person is left to fight alone or give up or call me, which is what generally happens, and lands on me to say, I'm not sure what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I was around for the development of Create NYC, which focused quite heavily on disability and access issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I attended town hall meetings, and from the plan, the Disability Forward Fund was created, where I served on one of the first panels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Today, that fund is a little understood add-on for accommodations with no review and no accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: We must acknowledge that very little has changed in terms of arts access policy in New York City in the last 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: The fund should return to its original purpose, with deaf and disabled people and access workers part of the decision-making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: But money alone isn't the answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: A grant can pay for one interpreter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: one time, but it can't make inclusion a standard rather than a courtesy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: The city can lead that change by building access into how it funds, plans, and measures culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Now I sit on the steering committee of Cultural Accessibility NYC, an initiative where once again we're reinventing the wheel to gather data on disability and access we couldn't get from DCLA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: The city should be our partner, not leave us to do this alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I'm asking for access reporting from city-funded cultural organizations, a plan to meet the city's goals, and above all, accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: As I'm nearing the end of my career, and I've run out of patience and energy for serving...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You can finish up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: I've run out of patience for energy for serving on committees without commitment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: But perhaps naively, I still have hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: So maybe for the last time, I'll ask you to work with us, ask us, include us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: But finally, let's do something to make real and lasting change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Prevor
utterances.text: Thank you.
