chapters.summary: Amilcar Priestley of the Afro-Latino Project and Afro-Latino Festival says reggaeton began with Afro-Caribbean communities in Panama translating Jamaican reggae into Spanish, traveled through Brooklyn, and was fused by Puerto Rican artists into a global genre.
chapters.title: Amilcar Priestley testifies for Resolution 625 and reggaeton's Panamanian roots

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Next, we have Amilcar.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairwoman Williams, members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: My name is Amrita Priestley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: I'm here on behalf of the Afro-Latino Project and the Afro-Latino Festival, and I'm here also representing the Panamanian community here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Thank you to Council members Lewis and co-sponsors Farias and Sanchez for bringing Resolution 625A to the floor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Reggaeton is one of the most popular genres on earth currently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Its story is often told as if it began in one place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: The truth is much richer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: In the late 1970s and 80s, Afro-Caribbean communities in Panama, many descended from West Indian workers who built the canal, began taking Jamaican reggae and putting it into Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: They called it reggae en español, or plena.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: It traveled by cassette, by radio, by Diablo Rojo bus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Artists such as El General, Renato, and many others carried that sound across borders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: It was influenced in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: It permeated many of Brooklyn's most popular venues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: And it was one of the seeds that germinated right here in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: That sound also reached Puerto Rico, and I want to be clear, Puerto Rican artists took it, fused it with hip-hop, and built it into the global force that we now see today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: This resolution enhances the contributions of both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: A shared...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Caribbean story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: It also honors New York, the city's mix of dancehall, hip-hop, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Latin communities helped shape the genre.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Reggaeton is part of who we are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: It's not the only time that Puerto Rico and Panama have come together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Carlos Russell, who you'll know, was one of the mentors of the Young Lords, as told by the famous Felipe Luciano.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: So this continues that important line of shared cultural heritage and shared political history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: For Panamanians, it's important for this resolution to pass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Many of our pioneers never received the credit or the rewards of the industry that they helped create.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Your time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Our African-American communities have too often been overlooked, even at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Recognition from the largest city in the country says that this history is important and it counts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Heritage Month gives schools, artists, and community groups a moment each October to tell this full story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: I respectfully urge the council to pass this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amilcar Priestley
utterances.text: Thank you once again.

summary: Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries and International Relations holds oversight hearing on 'What's Next for CreateNYC?' and several cultural resolutions.
DCLA Commissioner Diya Vij, IBO analyst Arden Armbruster, researchers, and dozens of public witnesses testify on cultural equity, funding, affordability, arts education, and disability access.

Chair Nantasha Williams and Council Members Stevens and Louis question witnesses on CDF/CIG funding, workforce diversity, affordable space, data transparency, and implementation of the 2017 cultural plan.
